Scientific Machine Learning:


Numerical Analysis

Physical laws are written as derivatives, integrals and differential equations, and a computer can handle none of these directly. Numerical analysis supplies the approximations that make them computable: roots of nonlinear equations, finite difference derivatives, numerical integration, and time-stepping schemes for ordinary and partial differential equations. These are the classical tools that scientific machine learning both competes with and builds on, and every one of them reappears later, inside a loss function or as the reference solution a network is compared against.


Learning Objectives¶

After studying this notebook, you should be able to

Roots of nonlinear equations

  • state the rootfinding problem $f(r) = 0$, and explain why the residual $f(\tilde r)$, not the error $\tilde r - r$, is the quantity a numerical method can actually measure;
  • apply the bisection method, write down its error bound after $k$ steps, and explain why it always converges and why it is nevertheless slow;
  • run a fixed-point iteration $x_{k+1} = g(x_k)$ and predict from $|g'(p)|$ whether it converges, and how fast;
  • derive Newton's method from the tangent line, implement it with sensible stopping criteria, and recognize its quadratic convergence in a table of errors;
  • derive the secant method, explain why it needs no derivative, and compare its cost per step with Newton's;
  • compare the three methods on the same equation in terms of iterations and function evaluations, and choose between them.

Finite difference derivatives

  • explain why a derivative must be approximated on a computer, and why the limit $\Delta x \to 0$ cannot simply be taken;
  • derive the forward, backward and central difference formulas from Taylor series, and read off the order of accuracy of each from the leading error term;
  • derive the central formula for the second derivative, and build a higher-order stencil by combining two lower-order ones;
  • measure an order of accuracy numerically from the slope of an error curve on a log-log plot;
  • differentiate a function sampled on a grid, and handle the two boundaries with one-sided formulas.

Numerical integration

  • explain why an integral must often be computed numerically, and recognize the Riemann sum hidden in the definition of the integral;
  • write down the left-sided and right-sided rectangle rules, implement both, and explain why they are first-order accurate;
  • obtain the trapezoidal rule as the average of the two rectangle rules, and explain why averaging raises the order from one to two;
  • estimate an area by hit-or-miss sampling and an integral by the sample mean, and explain why a uniform random sample turns an integral into an expected value;
  • state the $O(N^{-1/2})$ convergence rate of a Monte Carlo estimate, explain why it does not depend on the dimension, and say at which dimension it overtakes a grid-based rule.

Numerical solutions to ODEs

  • write a differential equation as a first-order system $\dot{x} = f(x)$ with an initial condition, and explain what a numerical solver actually produces;
  • derive the forward and backward Euler methods from the forward and backward difference formulas, and write both in matrix form for a linear system;
  • implement both methods as a loop and compare them with a library solver;
  • explain the difference between local and global error, and show why both Euler methods are first-order accurate;
  • determine, from $|1 + \lambda\Delta t|$ or from the eigenvalues of $I + \Delta t A$, whether a step size is stable, and explain why the implicit method has no such restriction;
  • set up and simulate a nonlinear system such as the pendulum, and recognize the signature of an unstable integrator in the result.

Boundary value problems

  • explain why a boundary value problem cannot be marched like an initial value problem, and why its unknowns must be solved for simultaneously;
  • discretize $u'' = f$ with the three-point central stencil and assemble the resulting tridiagonal system;
  • move the known boundary values to the right-hand side, solve the system, and confirm second-order accuracy by grid refinement;
  • state how a Neumann condition changes the system, and why the order of the boundary formula matters.

Partial differential equations

  • classify a second-order PDE as hyperbolic, parabolic or elliptic, and say which physical behaviour each describes;
  • derive the explicit FTCS scheme for the heat equation by combining a forward difference in time with a central difference in space;
  • state the stability condition $r = \alpha\Delta t/\Delta x^2 \le 1/2$, explain it both from the sign of the weight $1 - 2r$ and from the amplification factor, and recognize the sawtooth that appears when it is violated;
  • derive the implicit BTCS scheme, assemble the tridiagonal system it requires at every time step, and explain why it is unconditionally stable;
  • choose between an explicit and an implicit method for a given problem.

1. Roots of Nonlinear Equations¶

Setup

NumPy, Matplotlib and the SciPy routines used for reference solutions.

In [ ]:
%matplotlib inline
import numpy as np
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import root_scalar
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
from scipy.linalg import expm

1.1. The Root Finding Problem¶

1.1.1. Definition¶

Given a continuous function $f$ of one variable, the root finding problem is to find a real number $r$, called a root, such that


$$ f(r) = 0 . $$


Any equation of the form $g(x) = h(x)$ can be written in this standard form by setting $f = g - h$, so the definition is not restrictive.


Roots of a general $f$ cannot be computed exactly in finitely many arithmetic operations. Every method of this chapter is therefore iterative: it produces a sequence $x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots$ that (we hope) converges to $r$, and we stop when the sequence has settled down to the accuracy we need.

1.1.2. A Running Example¶

The methods of Sections 1.2, 1.4 and 1.5 are all compared on one equation,


$$ f(x) = x e^{x} - 2 = 0 , $$


so that they can be judged on equal terms. It cannot be solved in closed form with elementary functions, but a glance at the graph shows that $f$ is increasing on $[0, 1]$ with $f(0) = -2 < 0$ and $f(1) = e - 2 \approx 0.718 > 0$, so there is exactly one root in that interval.


The first code cell imports everything used below and plots $f$. The accurate reference value $r$ printed there is obtained with SciPy's root_scalar; we will use it only to measure the error of our own iterations, which is a luxury unavailable in a real computation.

In [ ]:
def f(x):
    return x*np.exp(x) - 2

# accurate reference value, used only to measure the error of our own iterations
r = root_scalar(f, bracket = [0, 1], xtol = 1e-15).root

print('reference root   r = %.5f' % r)
print('residual      f(r) = %.1e' % f(r))

reference root   r = 0.85261
residual      f(r) = 0.0e+00
In [ ]:
# Plot
xx = np.linspace(0, 1.5, 400)

plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(xx, f(xx), 'k', linewidth = 2)
plt.plot([0, 1.5], [0, 0], 'k', linewidth = 0.5)
plt.plot(r, 0, 'ro', markersize = 8)
plt.grid(alpha = 0.2)
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('f(x)')
plt.title('$f(x) = xe^x - 2$')
plt.show()

1.2. Bisection Method¶

1.2.1. The Idea¶

The bisection method rests on the intermediate value theorem: if $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and


$$ f(a)\,f(b) < 0 , $$


then $f$ changes sign on the interval, so $[a, b]$ contains at least one root. Such an interval is called a bracket.


The bisection method shrinks the bracket by halving it. Let $x_k$ be the midpoint of the current interval. Evaluating $f(x_k)$ tells us which half still has the sign change: if $f(a)$ and $f(x_k)$ have opposite signs the root lies in $[a, x_k]$, otherwise it lies in $[x_k, b]$. Replace the interval by that half and repeat. The bracket is never lost, so the method cannot fail.


The implementation below returns the sequence of midpoints, so that the convergence can be inspected afterwards. Each pass costs exactly one new evaluation of $f$.

In [ ]:
a = 0
b = 1

print('f(a) = %8.4f' % f(a))
print('f(b) = %8.4f' % f(b))

f(a) =  -2.0000
f(b) =   0.7183
In [ ]:
# Store initial bracket for bound calculation
a_initial = a
b_initial = b

# Initial setup
fa = f(a)
xb = []  # List to store history of midpoints

# Halve the bracket until it is narrow enough
while (b - a) / 2 > 1e-14:
    xm = (a + b) / 2
    fm = f(xm)
    xb.append(xm)

    # Check which half contains the sign change
    if np.sign(fm) == np.sign(fa):
        a = xm
        fa = fm  # Update f(a) for the next iteration
    else:
        b = xm

xb = np.array(xb)
errb = np.abs(xb - r)

# Display convergence history
print('%3s %15s %12s %12s' % ('k', 'x_k', '|error|', 'bound'))
print('-' * 46)

for k in range(min(10, len(xb))):
    bound = (b_initial - a_initial) / (2.0 ** (k + 1))  # 2^-(k+1) for unit interval
    print('%3d  %15.12f  %12.2e  %12.2e' % (k + 1, xb[k], errb[k], bound))

# Only print final error if xb is not empty
if len(xb) > 0:
    print('\nTotal steps: %s, Final error: %.2e' % (len(xb), errb[-1]))
else:
    print('\nNo steps were taken as the initial bracket was already narrow enough.')

  k             x_k      |error|        bound
----------------------------------------------
  1   0.500000000000      3.53e-01      5.00e-01
  2   0.750000000000      1.03e-01      2.50e-01
  3   0.875000000000      2.24e-02      1.25e-01
  4   0.812500000000      4.01e-02      6.25e-02
  5   0.843750000000      8.86e-03      3.12e-02
  6   0.859375000000      6.77e-03      1.56e-02
  7   0.851562500000      1.04e-03      7.81e-03
  8   0.855468750000      2.86e-03      3.91e-03
  9   0.853515625000      9.10e-04      1.95e-03
 10   0.852539062500      6.64e-05      9.77e-04

Total steps: 46, Final error: 5.11e-15

The first few midpoints are nowhere near the root — the method knows only the sign of $f$, never how close to zero it is — and the error column is not even monotone: step $4$ is worse than step $3$, and step $8$ worse than step $7$. What is monotone is the last column, the width of the bracket, which halves without fail. Every line of the table is therefore a guarantee rather than a hope, and the next subsection turns that guarantee into a formula.

1.2.2. Convergence¶

The initial bracket has width $b - a$; after $k$ halvings it has width $(b-a)/2^{k}$, and the midpoint $x_k$ is within half of that of the root:


$$ |x_k - r| \le \frac{b - a}{2^{k}} . $$


This is an error bound available before the computation starts. Solving for $k$ gives the number of steps needed for a required accuracy $\delta$,


$$ k \ge \log_2\!\frac{b - a}{\delta} , $$


independently of $f$. For $[a, b] = [0, 1]$ and $\delta = 10^{-14}$ this is $k \approx 46$ — and the loop above indeed stops after $46$ steps, with a final error of about $5 \times 10^{-15}$.


The error is (at worst) multiplied by $\tfrac12$ at every step, which is linear convergence with rate $\sigma = 1/2$: a straight line on a semilogarithmic plot, and about $\log_{10} 2^{-1} \approx 0.3$ decimal digits gained per iteration, i.e. one digit every $3.3$ evaluations of $f$. That rate is fixed: it can be beaten, but only by a method that looks at the values of $f$ and not merely at its sign.

In [ ]:
k = np.arange(1, len(xb) + 1)

plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.semilogy(k, errb, 'ko-', linewidth = 1.2, markersize = 3)
plt.semilogy(k, 2.0**(-k), 'r--', linewidth = 1.2)
plt.legend(['bisection error', 'bound $2^{-k}$'])
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('$k$')
plt.ylabel('$|x_k - r|$')
plt.show()

Remark (what bisection cannot do). It needs a bracket to start, and finding one requires some knowledge of the function — a plot, physical reasoning, or a scan over a grid. It also cannot find a root at which $f$ touches zero without crossing it, such as $x = 0$ for $f(x) = x^2$, because no bracket exists there. Finally, it uses only the sign of $f$, and therefore never converges faster than rate $1/2$ no matter how smooth or well-behaved the function is. The methods that follow use the values of $f$, gaining speed and losing the guarantee.


1.3. Fixed-Point Iteration¶

1.3.1. From Root Finding to a Fixed-Point Problem¶

We want to solve


$$ f(x) = 0 . $$


Instead of attacking this directly, we rewrite it as a fixed-point problem: find a point that a function maps to itself,


$$ x = g(x) . $$


A point $r$ with $r = g(r)$ is called a fixed point of $g$. The rewriting is always possible algebraically, for instance


$$ \begin{align*} x &= x + f(x) = g(x), \quad \text{or} \\ x &= x - f(x) = g(x) . \end{align*} $$


The choice of $g$ is not unique, and it is not innocent. Every valid rewriting has the same solution, but as the examples below show, some of them produce an iteration that converges quickly, some converge slowly, and some do not converge at all. Choosing $g$ well is the entire craft of this method.

The algorithm

  1. Choose an initial guess $x_0$.
  2. Repeat $x_{k+1} = g(x_k)$ until the change between successive iterates is small enough.

That is the whole method: evaluate the function, feed the answer back in, repeat. No derivatives, no linear systems, no bracketing.

1.3.2. When Does It Converge?¶

Let $r$ be the exact solution, so that $r = g(r)$, and define the error at step $k$ as $e_k = x_k - r$. Subtracting the two relations,


$$ \begin{aligned} x_{k+1} &= g(x_k) \\ r &= g(r) \\[4pt] e_{k+1} = x_{k+1} - r &= g(x_k) - g(r) . \end{aligned} $$


By the mean value theorem there is a point $\eta$ between $x_k$ and $r$ with


$$ g(x_k) - g(r) = g'(\eta)\,(x_k - r), $$


so the errors obey the simple recursion


$$ e_{k+1} = g'(\eta)\, e_k \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \lvert e_{k+1}\rvert \le \lvert g'(\eta)\rvert \cdot \lvert e_k \rvert . $$


Therefore, if $\lvert g'\rvert < 1$ near the root, every step shrinks the error by roughly that factor and the iteration converges. If $\lvert g'\rvert > 1$, every step enlarges the error and the iteration diverges.


$$ \text{converges if } \lvert g'(r)\rvert < 1, \qquad \text{diverges if } \lvert g'(r)\rvert > 1\ $$


Three further readings of this result are worth keeping in mind.

  • The convergence is linear: the error is multiplied by approximately the constant $\lvert g'(r)\rvert$ at every step, so the number of correct digits grows by a fixed amount per iteration. A smaller $\lvert g'(r)\rvert$ means faster convergence.

  • The special case $g'(r) = 0$ is much better than linear. The first-order term vanishes, the next term in the Taylor expansion takes over, and the error is then squared at each step. Section 1.3.4 contains an example.

  • The result is local. It describes the behaviour once the iterate is near $r$, where $g'(\eta)\approx g'(r)$. A poor starting point can still send the iteration somewhere else entirely.

The geometric picture

The condition has a picture that is worth more than the algebra. Plot $y = g(x)$ and the diagonal $y = x$ on the same axes. A fixed point is where the two curves cross.


Starting at $x_k$ on the horizontal axis, one iteration does two things: move vertically to the curve, which computes $g(x_k)$, and then move horizontally to the diagonal, which turns that value into the next input $x_{k+1}$. Repeating draws a staircase or a spiral, and whether it winds inward toward the crossing or outward away from it is decided by how steep $g$ is there compared with the diagonal. This is the cobweb diagram, and we draw it for every example below.

In [ ]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

A helper for the cobweb diagram. Given a function $g$, a starting point, and a number of steps, it plots $g$, the diagonal, and the alternating vertical and horizontal moves of the iteration.

In [ ]:
def cobweb(g, x0, n_steps, a, b, name):
    x = np.linspace(a, b, 200)

    plt.plot(x, g(x), 'b', linewidth = 2, label = name)
    plt.plot(x, x, 'k', linewidth = 1, label = 'y = x')

    xk = x0
    for k in range(n_steps):
        xn = g(xk)
        plt.plot([xk, xk], [xk, xn], 'r', linewidth = 1)   # vertical: evaluate g
        plt.plot([xk, xn], [xn, xn], 'r', linewidth = 1)   # horizontal: feed it back
        xk = xn

    plt.plot(x0, x0, 'ro')
    plt.xlabel('x');  plt.ylabel('y');  plt.legend();

1.3.3. Example: Solving $x = \cos(x)$¶

The equation $\cos(x) = x$ cannot be solved in closed form, but it is already in fixed-point form with $g(x) = \cos(x)$. First look at where the solution is.

In [ ]:
x = np.linspace(-1.5*np.pi, 1.5*np.pi, 100)

plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(x, np.cos(x), linewidth = 2, label = 'cos(x)')
plt.plot(x, x, linewidth = 2, label = 'x')
plt.axvline(x = 0, color = 'k', linestyle = '--')
plt.axhline(y = 0, color = 'k', linestyle = '--')
plt.axis('equal')
plt.ylim([-4, 4]);
plt.xlabel('x');
plt.legend();
plt.show()

The two curves cross exactly once, somewhere near $x = 0.74$. There is one solution and we now compute it.


A first attempt. The most direct way to express "apply $\cos$ again and again" is to write it out by hand.

In [ ]:
x = 0.3

print(np.cos(x))
print(np.cos(np.cos(x)))
print(np.cos(np.cos(np.cos(x))))
print(np.cos(np.cos(np.cos(np.cos(x)))))
print(np.cos(np.cos(np.cos(np.cos(np.cos(x))))))

0.955336489125606
0.5773340444711864
0.8379206831271269
0.6690097308223832
0.7844362247423562

The numbers are clearly settling down, alternating above and below some value near $0.74$. But writing one more line for every additional step is not a method. The same computation belongs in a loop.

In [ ]:
x = 0.3

for k in range(60):
    x = np.cos(x)

print(x)

0.739085133198378

Keeping the history. Overwriting x at every step throws away the information we most want to look at, which is how the iterate approaches its limit. Storing the sequence costs one array.

In [ ]:
n = 20
x = np.zeros(n)
x[0] = 0.3

for k in range(n-1):
    x[k+1] = np.cos(x[k])

for k in range(n):
    print('k = %2d   x = %.10f' % (k, x[k]))

k =  0   x = 0.3000000000
k =  1   x = 0.9553364891
k =  2   x = 0.5773340445
k =  3   x = 0.8379206831
k =  4   x = 0.6690097308
k =  5   x = 0.7844362247
k =  6   x = 0.7077866473
k =  7   x = 0.7598027553
k =  8   x = 0.7249718828
k =  9   x = 0.7485180672

k = 18   x = 0.7388149331
k = 19   x = 0.7392671163

Two features of this sequence are worth naming.


The iterates alternate around the solution: one is above, the next below. That is the sign of $g'$ at work. Here $g'(x) = -\sin(x)$ is negative near the root, so $e_{k+1} = g'e_k$ flips the sign of the error at every step.


The approach is steady rather than dramatic: each step removes a fixed fraction of the remaining error. That fraction should be $\lvert g'(r)\rvert = \lvert\sin(r)\rvert$, and the next cell checks it.

In [ ]:
r = 0.7390851332151607          # the fixed point, accurate to machine precision

print('r        = %.10f' % r)
print('cos(r)   = %.10f' % np.cos(r))
print('g\'(r)    = %.6f' % (-np.sin(r)))
print('|g\'(r)|  = %.6f   -> less than 1, so the iteration converges' % abs(np.sin(r)))

print('\n k      x_k          e_k        |e_k| / |e_k-1|')
x = 0.3
e_old = abs(x - r)
for k in range(1, 11):
    x = np.cos(x)
    e = abs(x - r)
    print('%2d   %.10f   %.3e      %.4f' % (k, x, e, e/e_old))
    e_old = e

r        = 0.7390851332
cos(r)   = 0.7390851332
g'(r)    = -0.673612
|g'(r)|  = 0.673612   -> less than 1, so the iteration converges

The ratio of successive errors hovers around $0.674$, which is exactly $\lvert g'(r)\rvert$. The theory of Section 1.3.2 is confirmed, and it also tells us the cost: since $0.674^{k}$ must reach $10^{-10}$, about $58$ iterations are needed for full double precision, and that number could have been predicted before running anything.


The cobweb diagram shows the same behaviour geometrically.

In [ ]:
plt.figure(figsize = (5, 5))
cobweb(np.cos, 0.3, 12, -0.2, 1.4, 'g(x) = cos(x)')
plt.show()

The path spirals inward toward the crossing point. Spiralling rather than climbing is the geometric form of the sign alternation noticed above, and the fact that it winds inward is the geometric form of $\lvert g'\rvert < 1$: the curve is flatter than the diagonal where they meet.


Does the starting point matter? The convergence result of Section 1.3.2 is local, so it is fair to ask what happens far from the root.

In [ ]:
x = 10.0

for k in range(60):
    x = np.cos(x)

print(x)

0.7390851332074554

It converges to the same value. This is a happy accident of this particular $g$: no matter where the iteration starts, the first step lands inside $[-1,1]$, because that is the range of the cosine, and from there $\lvert g'\rvert = \lvert\sin(x)\rvert \le \sin(1) \approx 0.84 < 1$ everywhere. The map is a contraction on an interval it cannot escape, so it converges from any starting point. Most fixed-point iterations are not this forgiving.

1.3.4. Example: Computing $\sqrt{2}$¶

Now take $f(x) = x^2 - 2$, whose positive root is $\sqrt{2}$. Rewriting as a fixed-point problem, the most obvious choice is to divide,


$$ x^2 = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = \frac{2}{x} = g(x) . $$


This is a correct rewriting: $\sqrt{2}$ certainly satisfies it. Let us iterate.

In [ ]:
x = 2.0

for k in range(10):
    x = 2/x
    print('k = %2d   x = %.10f' % (k + 1, x))

k =  1   x = 1.0000000000
k =  2   x = 2.0000000000
k =  3   x = 1.0000000000
k =  4   x = 2.0000000000
k =  5   x = 1.0000000000
k =  6   x = 2.0000000000
k =  7   x = 1.0000000000
k =  8   x = 2.0000000000
k =  9   x = 1.0000000000
k = 10   x = 2.0000000000

The iteration is trapped in a cycle: $2 \to 1 \to 2 \to 1 \to \cdots$, and it never approaches $\sqrt{2} = 1.4142\ldots$ at all. Section 1.3.2 explains why immediately:


$$ g(x) = \frac{2}{x} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad g'(x) = -\frac{2}{x^2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad g'(\sqrt{2}) = -\frac{2}{2} = -1 . $$


The magnitude is exactly $1$, the borderline case. The error is neither shrunk nor enlarged, only flipped in sign, so the iteration circles the solution forever without approaching it. The cobweb diagram makes this unmistakable.

In [ ]:
x = np.linspace(0.2, 4, 100)
g = lambda x: 2/x

cobweb(g, 2, 10, 0.2, 4, 'g(x) = 2/x')
plt.axis('equal')
plt.ylim([0, 4])
plt.show()

The cobweb closes into a rectangle instead of spiralling in. Nothing is wrong with the algebra; the rewriting is simply a bad one.


A better rewriting. The failure suggests its own cure. When the iterate is too small, $2/x$ overshoots to a value that is too large, and the other way round, so the true answer always lies between $x$ and $2/x$. Taking their average instead of jumping the whole way gives


$$ g(x) = \frac{1}{2}\left(x + \frac{2}{x}\right). $$


This is the same fixed point, since $x = (x + 2/x)/2$ still implies $x^2 = 2$, but a very different iteration.

In [ ]:
x = 3.0

for k in range(8):
    x = (x + 2/x)/2
    print('k = %2d   x = %.16f' % (k + 1, x))

print('\nnumpy sqrt(2) = %.16f' % np.sqrt(2))

k =  1   x = 1.8333333333333333
k =  2   x = 1.4621212121212122
k =  3   x = 1.4149984298948031
k =  4   x = 1.4142137800471977
k =  5   x = 1.4142135623731118
k =  6   x = 1.4142135623730949
k =  7   x = 1.4142135623730949
k =  8   x = 1.4142135623730949

numpy sqrt(2) = 1.4142135623730951

Six iterations reach machine precision, agreeing with NumPy's own square root to the last stored digit, from a starting point that was not even close. The reason is again in the derivative:


$$ g(x) = \frac{1}{2}\left(x + \frac{2}{x}\right) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad g'(x) = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 - \frac{2}{x^2}\right) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad g'(\sqrt{2}) = \frac{1}{2}(1-1) = 0 . $$


The derivative vanishes at the root. The linear term in the error recursion disappears, the quadratic term takes over, and the error is squared at every step rather than multiplied by a constant. That is why the number of correct digits roughly doubles per line in the output above: $1, 3, 6, 13$ and then machine precision.

Remark. This is not a lucky guess. Applying Newton's method to $f(x) = x^2-2$ gives $x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k)/f'(x_k) = x_k - (x_k^2-2)/(2x_k) = (x_k + 2/x_k)/2$, exactly the averaged iteration. Newton's method is a fixed-point iteration whose $g$ has been constructed so that $g'(r) = 0$, which is precisely why it converges quadratically. The averaging that looked like an ad hoc repair is the systematic construction in disguise.

In [ ]:
g_newton = lambda x: (x + 2/x)/2

cobweb(g_newton, 3.0, 6, 0.5, 3.5, 'g(x) = (x + 2/x)/2')
plt.axis('equal')
plt.show()

The staircase descends monotonically onto the crossing point, and the steps shorten so quickly that the last ones are invisible. Compare this with the closed rectangle of $g(x) = 2/x$: the same equation, the same solution, two different rewritings, and completely different behaviour.

1.3.5. Fixed-Point Iteration for Linear Systems¶

The same idea applies to systems of equations. Consider


$$ \begin{align*} 4x_1 - x_2 + x_3 &= 7 \\ 4x_1 - 8x_2 + x_3 &= -21 \\ -2x_1 + x_2 + 5x_3 &= 15 \end{align*} $$


For a system this small the direct solution is immediate.

In [ ]:
A = np.array([[4, -1, 1],
              [4, -8, 1],
              [-2, 1, 5]])
b = np.array([7, -21, 15])

x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(x)

[2. 4. 3.]

Direct solution is the right tool here, but it costs on the order of $n^3$ operations and it requires storing the whole matrix. For the large sparse systems that come out of discretized PDEs, with $n$ in the millions, iterative methods are preferred, and the simplest of them is the fixed-point iteration of this section.


To build it, solve each equation for the variable on its own diagonal:


$$ \begin{align*} 4x_1 - x_2 + x_3 = 7 \qquad &\Longrightarrow \qquad x_1 = \tfrac{1}{4}x_2 - \tfrac{1}{4}x_3 + \tfrac{7}{4}\\ 4x_1 - 8x_2 + x_3 = -21 \qquad &\Longrightarrow \qquad x_2 = \tfrac{1}{2}x_1 + \tfrac{1}{8}x_3 + \tfrac{21}{8}\\ -2x_1 + x_2 + 5x_3 = 15 \qquad &\Longrightarrow \qquad x_3 = \tfrac{2}{5}x_1 - \tfrac{1}{5}x_2 + 3 \end{align*} $$


Each equation now expresses one unknown in terms of the others, which is exactly the form $\mathbf{x} = G\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{c}$:


$$ \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{1}{4} & -\frac{1}{4}\\ \frac{1}{2} & 0 & \frac{1}{8}\\ \frac{2}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \frac{7}{4}\\ \frac{21}{8}\\ 3 \end{bmatrix} $$


and the iteration is the vector version of $x_{k+1} = g(x_k)$:


$$ \mathbf{x}^{(k+1)} = G\,\mathbf{x}^{(k)} + \mathbf{c} . $$


This particular choice, isolating each variable using its own diagonal entry, is known as the Jacobi method.

In [ ]:
G = np.array([[0,   1/4, -1/4],
              [1/2, 0,    1/8],
              [2/5, -1/5, 0  ]])
c = np.array([7/4, 21/8, 3])

x = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 2.0])      # initial guess

for k in range(20):
    x = G.dot(x) + c
    print('k = %2d   x = %s' % (k + 1, np.round(x, 8)))

k =  1   x = [1.5   3.375 3.2  ]
k =  2   x = [1.79375 3.775   2.925  ]
k =  3   x = [1.9625 3.8875 2.9625]
k =  4   x = [1.98125   3.9765625 3.0075   ]
k =  5   x = [1.99226562 3.9915625  2.9971875 ]
k =  6   x = [1.99859375 3.99578125 2.99859375]
k =  7   x = [1.99929688 3.99912109 3.00028125]
k =  8   x = [1.99970996 3.99968359 2.99989453]
k =  9   x = [1.99994727 3.9998418  2.99994727]
k = 10   x = [1.99997363 3.99996704 3.00001055]
k = 11   x = [1.99998912 3.99998813 2.99999604]
k = 12   x = [1.99999802 3.99999407 2.99999802]
k = 13   x = [1.99999901 3.99999876 3.0000004 ]
k = 14   x = [1.99999959 3.99999956 2.99999985]
k = 15   x = [1.99999993 3.99999978 2.99999993]
k = 16   x = [1.99999996 3.99999995 3.00000001]
k = 17   x = [1.99999998 3.99999998 2.99999999]
k = 18   x = [2.         3.99999999 3.        ]
k = 19   x = [2. 4. 3.]
k = 20   x = [2. 4. 3.]

The iterates settle onto $(2, 4, 3)$, the same answer the direct solve produced, using nothing but one matrix-vector product per step.

1.3.6. Convergence for Linear Iterations¶

For the linear case the convergence condition can be derived exactly, without the mean value theorem. Unroll the iteration:


$$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{x}^{(k+1)} &= G\mathbf{x}^{(k)} + \mathbf{c}\\ &= G\left(G\mathbf{x}^{(k-1)} + \mathbf{c}\right) + \mathbf{c} = G^{2}\mathbf{x}^{(k-1)} + G\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{c}\\ &\;\;\vdots\\ &= G^{k+1}\mathbf{x}^{(0)} + \left(G^{k} + \cdots + G + I\right)\mathbf{c} . \end{align*} $$


Everything hinges on the powers $G^{k}$. If they shrink to zero, the influence of the initial guess disappears and the second group converges to $(I-G)^{-1}\mathbf{c}$, which is the solution. If they grow, nothing converges.


Writing $G$ in terms of its eigenvalues shows what controls the powers: applying $G$ multiplies the component along each eigenvector by the corresponding eigenvalue $\lambda_i$, so applying it $k$ times multiplies that component by $\lambda_i^{k}$. Every component decays if and only if every eigenvalue has magnitude below one. Defining the spectral radius as the largest of those magnitudes,


$$ \rho(G) = \max_i \lvert \lambda_i \rvert , $$


the condition is


$$ \;\text{the iteration } \quad \mathbf{x}^{(k+1)} = G\mathbf{x}^{(k)} + \mathbf{c} \quad \text{ converges if and only if } \quad \rho(G) < 1\; $$


This is the matrix version of $\lvert g'(r)\rvert<1$, and $\rho(G)$ plays the role of $\lvert g'\rvert$: it is also the factor by which the error shrinks per iteration.

In [ ]:
eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvals(G)

print('eigenvalues of G :', np.round(eigenvalues, 4))
print('spectral radius  : %.4f   -> less than 1, so it converges' % max(abs(eigenvalues)))

eigenvalues of G : [ 0.3347+0.j     -0.1674+0.2899j -0.1674-0.2899j]
spectral radius  : 0.3347   -> less than 1, so it converges

The spectral radius is $0.33$, so each iteration removes about two thirds of the error, which matches the speed observed in Section 1.3.5.


A different rearrangement of the same system. Just as $\sqrt{2}$ had a good rewriting and a bad one, a linear system can be rearranged in more than one way. Using $x = x + f(x)$ or $x = x - f(x)$ row by row instead of dividing by the diagonal gives


$$ \begin{align*} x_1 &= -3x_1 + x_2 - x_3 + 7\\ x_2 &= 4x_1 - 7x_2 + x_3 + 21\\ x_3 &= 2x_1 - x_2 - 4x_3 + 15 \end{align*} $$


Substituting $(2,4,3)$ confirms that this has the same solution as before. Now iterate it.

In [ ]:
G2 = np.array([[-3,  1, -1],
               [ 4, -7,  1],
               [ 2, -1, -4]])
c2 = np.array([7, 21, 15])

x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 2.0])

for k in range(10):
    x = G2.dot(x) + c2
    print('k = %2d   x = %s' % (k + 1, np.round(x, 2)))

k =  1   x = [ 4. 13.  7.]
k =  2   x = [  1. -47. -18.]
k =  3   x = [-25. 336. 136.]
k =  4   x = [  282. -2295.  -915.]
k =  5   x = [-2219. 16299.  6534.]
k =  6   x = [  16429. -116414.  -46858.]
k =  7   x = [-118836.  833777.  336719.]
k =  8   x = [  853573. -5975043. -2418310.]
k =  9   x = [-6117445. 42821304. 17355444.]
k = 10   x = [ 4.38182020e+07 -3.06863443e+08 -1.24477955e+08]

The solution is unchanged, and the iteration is useless: within ten steps the iterates have passed $10^{8}$. The spectral radius says why.

In [ ]:
eigenvalues2 = np.linalg.eigvals(G2)

print('eigenvalues of G2 :', np.round(eigenvalues2, 4))
print('spectral radius   : %.4f   -> greater than 1, so it diverges' % max(abs(eigenvalues2)))

eigenvalues of G2 : [-7.1642 -2.6086 -4.2271]
spectral radius   : 7.1642   -> greater than 1, so it diverges

Every eigenvalue lies outside the unit circle, the largest with magnitude $7.16$, so each iteration multiplies the error by roughly seven. After ten steps that is a factor of $7^{10}\approx 3\times10^{8}$, which is what the output shows.


1.4. Newton's Method¶

1.4.1. The Idea: Follow the Tangent¶

Section 1.3 solved $f(x)=0$ by rewriting it as $x=g(x)$ and iterating, and found that everything depended on a choice we made by hand. A good $g$ converged quickly, a bad one cycled forever, and there was no systematic recipe for producing a good one.


Newton's method is that recipe. Instead of guessing a rearrangement, it builds one from the function itself, using the only information available at a point: the value there and the slope there.


Suppose the current guess is $x_k$. Expand $f$ about that point and keep the linear term,


$$ f(x) \approx f(x_k) + f'(x_k)\,(x - x_k) . $$


This straight line is the tangent to $f$ at $x_k$. We cannot solve $f(x)=0$, but we can certainly solve the tangent equal to zero:


$$ f(x_k) + f'(x_k)\,(x_{k+1} - x_k) = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \;x_{k+1} = x_k - \frac{f(x_k)}{f'(x_k)}\; $$


The geometric statement. Stand on the curve at $x_k$, slide down the tangent line until it crosses the axis, and take that crossing as the next guess. Repeat. Where the curve is well approximated by its tangent, which is to say near a simple root, the crossing of the tangent is very close to the crossing of the curve, and the method converges extremely fast.


The price. The formula needs $f'$, which the fixed-point iteration of Section 1.3 did not. It must be derived by hand, obtained by automatic differentiation, or approximated. It must also not vanish: the method divides by it.

1.4.2. Newton's Method Is a Fixed-Point Iteration¶

Newton's method is not a new kind of algorithm. Reading the update as $x_{k+1}=g(x_k)$ identifies its map,


$$ g(x) = x - \frac{f(x)}{f'(x)} , $$


so everything proved in Section 1.3.2 applies. In particular the speed of convergence is decided by $g'$ at the root, and that derivative is worth computing. Differentiating with the quotient rule,


$$ g'(x) = 1 - \frac{f'(x)f'(x) - f(x)f''(x)}{\left[f'(x)\right]^2} = \frac{f(x)\,f''(x)}{\left[f'(x)\right]^2} . $$


Now evaluate at a simple root $r$, meaning one where $f(r)=0$ and $f'(r)\neq0$. The numerator contains the factor $f(r)$, which is zero, and the denominator is not zero. Therefore


$$ g'(r) = 0\; $$


This single line explains everything about the method. Section 1.3.2 observed that $g'(r)=0$ is the exceptional case in which the linear error term disappears and convergence becomes faster than linear. Newton's method is the construction that produces that case on purpose, for any $f$. The averaging trick that repaired the $\sqrt{2}$ iteration in Section 1.3.4 was not an isolated piece of cleverness; it was this formula applied to $f(x)=x^2-2$.


Notice also what the derivation assumed. If $f'(r)=0$, the root is not simple, the cancellation above fails, and the argument collapses. At such a root the method still converges, but only linearly.

1.4.3. Quadratic Convergence¶

To see how fast "faster than linear" is, expand the error one term further than Section 1.3.2 did. Write $e_k = x_k - r$ and expand $f$ and $f'$ about the root:


$$ f(x_k) = f'(r)\,e_k + \tfrac{1}{2}f''(r)\,e_k^2 + \cdots, \qquad f'(x_k) = f'(r) + f''(r)\,e_k + \cdots . $$


Substituting into $e_{k+1} = e_k - f(x_k)/f'(x_k)$ and keeping terms through $e_k^2$ gives


$$ e_{k+1} \approx \frac{f''(r)}{2f'(r)}\;e_k^{2} $$


The error is squared at every step, not multiplied by a constant. This is quadratic convergence, and its practical meaning is that the number of correct digits doubles per iteration: a guess good to two digits becomes good to four, then eight, then sixteen, at which point double precision is exhausted. Three or four iterations from a reasonable starting point is typical, and it is why Newton's method is the default for nonlinear problems throughout computational engineering.


The constant in front is not negligible but it is rarely decisive, because squaring the error overwhelms it after a step or two. It does say something useful, though: convergence is fastest where the curve is straightest near the root, since $f''(r)$ small means the tangent line is a good model over a wide neighbourhood.

The test problem. Take the transcendental equation


$$ f(x) = x\,e^{x} - 2 = 0 . $$


It cannot be solved by algebra: the unknown appears both as a factor and inside an exponent, and no rearrangement separates the two. Equations of this shape are common in engineering, arising whenever a linear effect multiplies an exponential one, as in thermal, chemical-kinetic and semiconductor problems.


The derivatives follow from the product rule,


$$ f'(x) = e^{x} + x\,e^{x} = (1+x)\,e^{x}, \qquad f''(x) = (2+x)\,e^{x} , $$


and both are positive for $x>0$, so there $f$ is increasing and convex. Since $f(0)=-2<0$ and $f(1)=e-2>0$, there is exactly one positive root, lying between $0$ and $1$. Its exact value is the Lambert $W$ function evaluated at $2$, $r = W(2) = 0.8526055020137254$, which we use only as a reference for measuring error.


The error law predicts the constant


$$ \frac{f''(r)}{2f'(r)} = \frac{(2+r)e^{r}}{2(1+r)e^{r}} = \frac{2+r}{2(1+r)} = 0.7699 , $$


the exponential cancelling. The next cell starts deliberately far away, at $x_0 = 2$.

In [ ]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
In [ ]:
def f(x):
    return x*np.exp(x) - 2

def dfdx(x):
    return (1 + x)*np.exp(x)

r = 0.8526055020137254           # the root, W(2), accurate to machine precision

x = 2.0
e_old = abs(x - r)

print(' k        x_k                  e_k         e_k / e_(k-1)^2')
for k in range(1, 9):
    x = x - f(x)/dfdx(x)
    e = abs(x - r)
    if e > 0:
        print('%2d   %.16f   %.3e      %.4f' % (k, x, e, e/e_old**2))
        e_old = e
    else:
        print('%2d   %.16f   %.3e      (exact)' % (k, x, e))

print('\npredicted constant  f\'\'(r) / (2 f\'(r)) = %.4f' % ((2 + r)/(2*(1 + r))))

 k        x_k                  e_k         e_k / e_(k-1)^2
 1   1.4235568554910751   5.710e-01      0.4337
 2   1.0349357885396127   1.823e-01      0.5593
 3   0.8755020570956831   2.290e-02      0.6887
 4   0.8530032869175266   3.978e-04      0.7588
 5   0.8526056238046466   1.218e-07      0.7697
 6   0.8526055020137370   1.155e-14      0.7784
 7   0.8526055020137254   0.000e+00      (exact)
 8   0.8526055020137254   0.000e+00      (exact)

predicted constant  f''(r) / (2 f'(r)) = 0.7699

Two phases are visible, and the separation between them is the lesson.


The first three steps are not fast. Starting at $x_0=2$ the error falls only from $1.15$ to $5.7\times10^{-1}$, $1.8\times10^{-1}$, $2.3\times10^{-2}$, roughly a factor of three per step, because the tangent at $x=2$ is a poor model of a curve that is bending sharply there. This is the approach phase, and no theory of this section governs it.


From the fourth step on the behaviour changes completely: $4.0\times10^{-4}$, $1.2\times10^{-7}$, $1.2\times10^{-14}$, then exact. Two correct digits become four, then seven, then fourteen, then all of them. Once the iterate is close enough for the quadratic law to hold, four steps exhaust double precision.


The ratio column confirms the law numerically. It drifts upward through the approach phase and then settles on $0.7697$, matching the predicted $(2+r)/\bigl(2(1+r)\bigr)=0.7699$ to three digits. That constant was computed from the analytic derivatives alone, before any iteration was run.

Comparison with a fixed-point iteration. The same equation can be rearranged in the manner of Section 1.3. Dividing $x e^{x}=2$ by $e^{x}$ gives


$$ x = 2e^{-x} \;\equiv\; g(x), \qquad g'(x) = -2e^{-x} . $$


At the root, $2e^{-r}=r$ by the equation itself, so $g'(r) = -r = -0.8526$. Its magnitude is less than one, so by the criterion of Section 1.3.2 the iteration converges, and the negative sign means it alternates about the root. But $0.85$ is uncomfortably close to $1$: each step removes only $15\%$ of the error, so roughly fifteen iterations are needed per decimal digit.

In [ ]:
# fixed-point iteration x <- 2 exp(-x)
x = 2.0
fixed_point_errors = []

for k in range(10):
    x = 2*np.exp(-x)
    fixed_point_errors.append(abs(x - r))

# Newton's method on f(x) = x exp(x) - 2
x = 2.0
newton_errors = []
for k in range(10):
    x = x - f(x)/dfdx(x)
    newton_errors.append(abs(x - r))

floor = 1e-17          # so that exact zeros can be drawn on a log axis

plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.semilogy(np.maximum(fixed_point_errors, floor), 'b', linewidth = 2, label = 'fixed point : x = 2 exp(-x)')
plt.semilogy(np.maximum(newton_errors, floor), 'rs-', label = 'Newton : f(x) = x exp(x) - 2')
plt.xlabel('iteration k');  plt.ylabel('|error|');  plt.legend();  plt.show()

On a logarithmic axis, linear convergence is a straight line and quadratic convergence is a curve that bends downward ever more steeply. The fixed-point iteration descends at a constant slope and needs $221$ steps to reach machine precision; Newton's method falls off the bottom of the plot in seven, so far to the left that its curve is pressed against the axis. The two methods are solving the same equation from the same starting point.

1.4.4. The Geometric Picture¶

The algebra is short enough that the geometry is easy to lose sight of. The next figure draws the first three tangent lines explicitly, starting again from $x_0 = 2$.

In [ ]:
xs = np.linspace(0.4, 2.2, 200)

plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(xs, f(xs), 'k', linewidth = 2, label = r'$f(x) = x e^x - 2$')
plt.axhline(y = 0, color = 'k', linewidth = 1)

x = 2.0
for k in range(3):
    slope = dfdx(x)
    x_new = x - f(x)/slope
    seg = np.linspace(x_new - 0.15, x + 0.1, 20)

    plt.plot(seg, f(x) + slope*(seg - x), 'r', alpha = 0.7)
    plt.plot([x, x], [0, f(x)], 'k--', alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 1)
    plt.plot(x, f(x), 'ro', markersize = 5)
    plt.plot(x_new, 0, 'r')
    plt.text(x + 0.03, -1.0, '$x_%s$' % k)
    x = x_new

plt.plot(r, 0, 'ko', markersize = 5)
plt.xlim([0.4, 2.2]);  plt.ylim([-3, 14])
plt.xlabel('x');  plt.ylabel('f(x)');  plt.legend();  plt.show()

Read the figure as a sequence. Each circle is the current iterate lifted onto the curve, each red line is the tangent there, and each cross is where that tangent meets the axis, which becomes the next iterate.


The picture explains both phases of the table. Far to the right the curve is strongly convex, the tangent lies well below it, and the crossing at $x_1 = 1.424$ falls far short of the root. The second tangent, taken on a gentler part of the curve, lands at $x_2 = 1.035$, much closer. By the third the curve is nearly straight over the remaining distance, the tangent is almost indistinguishable from it, and the crossing at $x_3 = 0.876$ already sits on the star.


Two features of the geometry are worth naming. Because $f$ is convex and increasing here, every tangent line lies below the curve, so every crossing falls to the right of the root and the iterates approach from one side only. And the horizontal distances from the crosses to the star, $0.57$, $0.18$, $0.023$, are exactly the errors of the table: the figure and the table are two views of the same three steps.

1.4.5. Newton's Method for Systems¶

Nothing in the derivation was one-dimensional. Given $n$ equations in $n$ unknowns,


$$ \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}, \qquad \mathbf{F} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n , $$


expand about the current iterate and keep the linear term. The role of the derivative is taken by the Jacobian matrix, the matrix of all first partial derivatives,


$$ J_{ij}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\partial F_i}{\partial x_j} , \qquad \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) \approx \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_k) + J(\mathbf{x}_k)\,(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_k) , $$


and setting the linear model to zero gives the multivariable update


$$ J(\mathbf{x}_k)\,\Delta\mathbf{x} = -\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_k), \qquad \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k + \Delta\mathbf{x} $$


Two points deserve emphasis. Division by $f'$ has become the solution of a linear system, so every Newton step for a system costs one matrix factorization, which is where the linear solvers of the numerical analysis material earn their place. And one should never form $J^{-1}$: solving $J\,\Delta\mathbf{x}=-\mathbf{F}$ is both cheaper and more accurate than computing an inverse and multiplying by it.


Test problem. Find where a circle and a parabola intersect,


$$ \begin{align*} x^2 + y^2 &= 4\\ y &= x^2 \end{align*} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{F}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix} x^2+y^2-4 \\ y-x^2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad J=\begin{bmatrix} 2x & 2y \\ -2x & 1 \end{bmatrix}. $$

In [ ]:
def F(v):
    x, y = v
    return np.array([x**2 + y**2 - 4,
                     y - x**2])

def Jacobian(v):
    x, y = v
    return np.array([[ 2*x, 2*y],
                     [-2*x, 1.0]])

v = np.array([1.0, 1.0])            # initial guess

print(' k      x            y          |F(v)|')
for k in range(5):
    delta = np.linalg.solve(Jacobian(v), -F(v))
    v = v + delta
    print('%2d   %.10f   %.10f   %.3e' % (k + 1, v[0], v[1], np.linalg.norm(F(v))))

y_exact = (-1 + np.sqrt(17))/2
print('\nexact :  x = %.10f   y = %.10f' % (np.sqrt(y_exact), y_exact))

 k      x            y          |F(v)|
 1   1.3333333333   1.6666666667   5.666e-01
 2   1.2532051282   1.5641025641   1.812e-02
 3   1.2496268211   1.5615543876   2.316e-05
 4   1.2496210677   1.5615528128   4.860e-11
 5   1.2496210677   1.5615528128   2.220e-16

exact :  x = 1.2496210677   y = 1.5615528128

The residual falls as $5.7\times10^{-1}$, $1.8\times10^{-2}$, $2.3\times10^{-5}$, $4.9\times10^{-11}$, and then round-off: the same doubling of correct digits as in one dimension. Eliminating $y$ by hand gives $x^2+x^4=4$, so the exact intersection has $y=(\sqrt{17}-1)/2$ and $x=\sqrt{y}$, which the last line confirms.

In [ ]:
theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 200)
xs = np.linspace(-2.2, 2.2, 200)

plt.figure(figsize = (5, 5))
plt.plot(2*np.cos(theta), 2*np.sin(theta), 'k', linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.6, label = r'$x^2 + y^2 = 4$')
plt.plot(xs, xs**2, 'k', linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.6, label = r'$y = x^2$')

v = np.array([1.0, 0.5])
path = [v]
for k in range(2):
    v = v + np.linalg.solve(Jacobian(v), -F(v))
    path.append(v)
path = np.array(path)

plt.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], 'ro', markersize = 3, label = 'Newton iterates')
plt.xlim([-2.5, 2.5]);  plt.ylim([-2.5, 2.5])
plt.grid(alpha = 0.3)
plt.xlabel('x');  plt.ylabel('y');  plt.legend();  plt.show()

The iterates start off both curves and move onto their intersection within two visible steps. Which of the two intersections is found depends entirely on the starting guess; beginning at $(-1,1)$ would have produced the mirror solution. Newton's method finds a root, never the roots, and in a system with many solutions the initial guess is what selects among them.

1.4.6. Bisection, Fixed Point, and Newton¶

Newton's method answers the question left open at the end of Section 1.3: how to choose the fixed-point map $g$ rather than guess it. The answer, $g = x - f/f'$, is constructed so that $g'(r)=0$ at every simple root, which is exactly the condition that makes convergence quadratic instead of linear.


What is gained is speed, and the margin is not small. On the same equation, plain fixed-point iteration needed about sixty steps where Newton needed four, and in the system of Section 1.4.5 the residual went from $10^{-1}$ to round-off in four steps.


What is given up is robustness. Fixed-point iteration with $\lvert g'\rvert<1$ converges from anywhere in the region where that bound holds; Newton's method carries no such guarantee: its convergence is only local, a step landing where $f'$ is near zero can be thrown far across the domain, and at a multiple root the rate drops back to linear. It also requires a derivative, or a Jacobian for a system, and a linear solve at every step.


The practical conclusion is the one every numerical library implements: use a slow and safe method to get close, then switch to Newton to finish. Bisection to locate, Newton to converge.


1.5. The Secant Method¶

1.5.1. Derivation and Implementation¶

Newton's method needs $f'$, which may be unavailable, expensive, or tedious to derive. The secant method replaces the tangent line by the line through the last two points $(x_{k-1}, f(x_{k-1}))$ and $(x_k, f(x_k))$, i.e. it approximates $f'(x_k)$ by a difference quotient:


$$ \begin{align*} f'(x_k) &\approx \frac{f(x_k)-f(x_{k-1})}{x_k - x_{k-1}}\\\\ x_{k+1} &= x_k - \frac{f(x_k)\,(x_k - x_{k-1})}{f(x_k) - f(x_{k-1})}, \qquad k = 2, 3, \dots \end{align*} $$


Two starting values $x_1, x_2$ are needed, and each iteration costs only one new function evaluation, since $f(x_{k-1})$ is remembered from the previous step.


Because the secant slope is only an approximation of the tangent slope, the convergence is not quite quadratic; the error obeys $|\epsilon_{k+1}| \approx c\,|\epsilon_k|^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha = (1 + \sqrt 5)/2 \approx 1.618$, the golden ratio. This is called superlinear convergence: slower than Newton per iteration, but each iteration is half the work, since Newton needs both $f$ and $f'$.

In [ ]:
x1 = 1.0
x2 = 0.5
xs = [x1, x2]

# take secant steps until the residual is negligible
while abs(f(x2)) > 1e-12:
    x3 = x2 - f(x2)*(x2 - x1)/(f(x2) - f(x1))
    x1 = x2
    x2 = x3
    xs.append(x2)

xs = np.array(xs)
errs = np.abs(xs - r)

print('  k        x_k             |error|      log|e_k+1|/log|e_k|')
for k in range(len(xs)):
    if k + 1 < len(xs):
        ratio = np.log(errs[k+1])/np.log(errs[k])
        print('%3d   %.12f   %9.2e      %6.3f' % (k + 1, xs[k], errs[k], ratio))
    else:
        print('%3d   %.12f   %9.2e' % (k + 1, xs[k], errs[k]))

2. Finite Difference Derivatives¶

2.1. Why Numerical Derivatives?¶

2.1.1. Motivation¶

Differentiation is taught as a symbolic operation: given a formula for $f$, the rules of calculus produce a formula for $f'$. On a computer that route is frequently unavailable.

  • The function is known only at sampled points — a sensor record, a table of measurements, the output of an experiment. There is no formula to differentiate.
  • The function is the output of a simulation or a black box — a finite-element solver, a legacy subroutine — that returns a number for each input and nothing else.
  • The derivative is needed at many points of a grid, as the building block of a numerical method for a differential equation. Discretizing $\partial u/\partial t = \alpha\, \partial^2 u/\partial x^2$ means replacing both derivatives by differences of grid values; this is the origin of the name finite difference method.

In each case we need a rule that turns values of $f$ into an approximation of $f'$, together with an honest statement of how wrong that approximation is.

2.1.2. The Limit That Cannot Be Taken¶

The definition of the derivative,


$$ f'(x) = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x} , $$


already suggests the approximation: stop before the limit and use a small but finite $\Delta x$. That single decision — the finite in finite difference — is the source of everything that follows.


Two questions arise immediately, and they pull in opposite directions. How large is the error committed by stopping at a finite $\Delta x$? It shrinks as $\Delta x$ shrinks, so we want $\Delta x$ small. But the numerator $f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)$ is a difference of two nearly equal numbers, and in floating-point arithmetic such a difference loses significant digits; dividing the damaged numerator by a tiny $\Delta x$ magnifies the damage. So we also want $\Delta x$ not small. The sections that follow study the first of these two errors.


Throughout we use the test function


$$ f(x) = \sin x , \qquad f'(x) = \cos x , \qquad f''(x) = -\sin x , $$


whose derivatives are known exactly, so that every approximation can be compared with the truth. All derivatives of $\sin$ are bounded by $1$, which will make the error estimates especially clean.


2.2. Forward and Backward Differences¶

2.2.1. Derivation from Taylor Series¶

Everything in this chapter comes from two expansions, one step to the right and one step to the left:


$$ (*)\qquad f(x + \Delta x) = f(x) + \Delta x\, f'(x) + \frac{\Delta x^2}{2!}f''(x) + \frac{\Delta x^3}{3!}f'''(x) + \cdots $$

$$ (**)\qquad f(x - \Delta x) = f(x) - \Delta x\, f'(x) + \frac{\Delta x^2}{2!}f''(x) - \frac{\Delta x^3}{3!}f'''(x) + \cdots $$


Solving $(*)$ for $f'(x)$ and dividing by $\Delta x$ gives the forward difference,


$$ \frac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x} = f'(x) + \frac{\Delta x}{2!}f''(x) + \frac{\Delta x^2}{3!}f'''(x) + \cdots $$


The expression tells us both that the left-hand side approximates $f'(x)$ and by how much it misses:


$$ D_{+}f(x) = \frac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x}, \qquad D_{+}f(x) - f'(x) = \frac{\Delta x}{2}f''(x) + O(\Delta x^2) . $$


The error is proportional to the first power of $\Delta x$; the formula is said to be first-order accurate, or of order $O(\Delta x)$. Halving $\Delta x$ halves the error.


The same treatment of $(**)$ gives the backward difference


$$ D_{-}f(x) = \frac{f(x) - f(x - \Delta x)}{\Delta x}, \qquad D_{-}f(x) - f'(x) = -\frac{\Delta x}{2}f''(x) + O(\Delta x^2) , $$


also first-order accurate. The two leading error terms are equal in size and opposite in sign — a fact that Section 2.3 exploits.


Remark (geometry). The forward difference is the slope of the line joining $(x, f(x))$ to the point one step to the right; the backward difference uses the point one step to the left. The tangent line at $x$ lies between them, which is exactly what the opposite signs of the two error terms say.

2.2.2. The Two Slopes at a Point¶

The three formulas are evaluated below at $x_0 = 1$ with a deliberately large step $\Delta x = 0.25$, so that the differences between them are easy to see. The figure draws the three sample points $x - \Delta x$, $x$ and $x + \Delta x$ together with the central-difference line through the outer two.

In [ ]:
x0 = 1
dx = .25

# Forward Difference Approximation
dfdxF = (np.sin(x0 + dx) - np.sin(x0)) / dx

# Backward Difference Approximation
dfdxB = (np.sin(x0) - np.sin(x0 - dx)) / dx

dfdxC = (np.sin(x0 + dx) - np.sin(x0 - dx)) / (2*dx)

print('exact       %8.5f' % np.cos(x0))
print('forward     %8.5f    error %8.5f' % (dfdxF, dfdxF - np.cos(x0)))
print('backward    %8.5f    error %8.5f' % (dfdxB, dfdxB - np.cos(x0)))

exact        0.54030
forward      0.43005    error -0.11025
backward     0.63933    error  0.09903

plt.plot(xs, np.sin(x0) + dfdxF*(xs - x0), 'b', linewidth = 1.2)          # Forward Difference
plt.plot(xs, np.sin(x0) + dfdxB*(xs - x0), 'g', linewidth = 1.2)          # Backward Difference
# plt.plot(xs, np.sin(x0) + dfdxC*(xs - x0), 'm', linewidth=1.2)          # Central Difference
plt.plot([x0 - dx, x0, x0 + dx], np.sin([x0 - dx, x0, x0 + dx]), 'ro', markersize = 4)
plt.plot([x0 - dx, x0 - dx], [0, np.sin(x0 - dx)], 'k--', alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 1)
plt.plot([x0, x0], [0, np.sin(x0)], 'k--', alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 1)
plt.plot([x0 + dx, x0 + dx], [0, np.sin(x0 + dx)], 'k--', alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 1)

plt.text(x0 - dx + 0.03, 0.52, r'$x - \Delta x$')
plt.text(x0 + dx + 0.03, 0.52, r'$x + \Delta x$')
# plt.legend(['Function', 'Exact Tangent', 'Forward Diff', 'Backward Diff'])
plt.ylim(0.5, 1.15)
plt.show()

The forward slope is too small by $0.110$ and the backward slope too large by $0.099$ — opposite in sign and both close to the predicted magnitude $\tfrac{\Delta x}{2}|f''(x_0)| = 0.105$. The true tangent therefore lies between the two secant slopes, as the remark predicted, and the central difference — the line drawn in the figure — is their average.


2.3. The Central Difference¶

2.3.1. Derivation¶

The forward and backward differences have leading errors $+\tfrac{\Delta x}{2}f''$ and $-\tfrac{\Delta x}{2}f''$. Averaging the two formulas must therefore cancel that term. Equivalently, and more systematically, subtract $(**)$ from $(*)$. Every term of even order is identical in the two expansions and cancels:


$$ f(x + \Delta x) - f(x - \Delta x) = 2\Delta x\, f'(x) + \frac{2\Delta x^3}{3!}f'''(x) + O(\Delta x^5) $$


Dividing by $2\Delta x$ gives the central difference


$$ D_{0}f(x) = \frac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x - \Delta x)}{2\Delta x}, \qquad D_{0}f(x) - f'(x) = \frac{\Delta x^2}{3!}f'''(x) + O(\Delta x^4) . $$


The formula is second-order accurate: halving $\Delta x$ divides the error by four. It costs the same two function evaluations as the forward difference, so the extra accuracy is free — the only price is that it needs a point on each side, which rules it out in two common situations: when $f'$ must be computed in real time, where the future value $f(x + \Delta x)$ is not yet available, and at the two ends of a finite data record (Section 2.5).


Intuition (why symmetry pays). The cancellation was not an accident of algebra. A symmetric formula cannot distinguish left from right, so its error cannot contain any term that changes sign when $\Delta x \to -\Delta x$ — that is, no odd power of $\Delta x$. Symmetry alone forces the error to start at $\Delta x^2$. The same argument explains why every symmetric stencil below has an even order of accuracy.

2.3.2. Comparing the Three Approximations¶

The tangent picture of Section 2.2.2 was drawn at a single point. A more revealing experiment applies the three formulas at every point of an interval and plots the results against the exact derivative. Take $f = \sin$ on $[-2, 4]$ with a coarse $\Delta t = 0.2$, so that the differences between the schemes are visible to the eye.

In [ ]:
dt = .2
t = np.linspace(-2, 4, 60)
f = np.sin(t)

# Exact Derivative
dfdt = np.cos(t)
In [ ]:

plt.grid(True)

plt.legend(['Function', 'Exact Derivative'], fontsize = 14)
plt.xlim(-2, 4)
plt.ylim(-1.5, 1.5)

   forward     0.09979

max | forward  - cos(t + dt/2) |    0.00166
