The zoomed panel shows what the error formulas predicted. The forward curve lies to the left of the exact derivative and the backward curve to the right, each by about half a step, and the printed check confirms it: the forward curve agrees with $\cos(t + \Delta t/2)$ sixty times better than with $\cos t$ itself. A forward difference is really the derivative evaluated near the midpoint $t + \Delta t/2$, not at $t$. The central curve is the average of the two, so the shifts cancel; it sits on top of the exact derivative and is hard to see at all, with an error fifteen times smaller than the other two.


Note also that the central curve has a slightly smaller amplitude than $\cos t$, and the measured ratio $0.9934$ is the factor $1 - \Delta t^2/6 = 0.9933$ that the error term predicts. A difference quotient over a finite step averages the function's variation across that step, and averaging always shaves the peaks. This is why finite differences act as mild low-pass filters on the data they are applied to.


2.4. Second Derivatives and Higher-Order Stencils¶

2.4.1. The Second Derivative¶

One route to $f''$ is to apply a difference formula twice: $f''$ is the derivative of $f'$, so


$$ f''(x) \approx \frac{f'(x + \Delta x) - f'(x)}{\Delta x} , $$


with each $f'$ replaced in turn by a difference of $f$ values. Any of the three schemes can be used, but it is important to be consistent and use the same scheme for both terms, or the orders of accuracy will not combine as expected.


The direct route is shorter. The central difference came from subtracting the two Taylor expansions; adding them cancels the odd terms instead:


$$ f(x + \Delta x) + f(x - \Delta x) = 2f(x) + \Delta x^2 f''(x) + \frac{\Delta x^4}{4!}f''''(x) + O(\Delta x^6) $$


Solving for $f''(x)$ gives the standard three-point formula


$$ \frac{f(x + \Delta x) - 2f(x) + f(x - \Delta x)}{\Delta x^2} = f''(x) + O(\Delta x^2) , $$


second-order accurate, and exactly what the two-stage route produces when central differences are used at both stages. Written on a grid with $f_k = f(x_k)$ and uniform spacing $\Delta x$, the two workhorse formulas of the finite difference method are


$$ f'(x_k) \approx \frac{f_{k+1} - f_{k-1}}{2\Delta x}, \qquad f''(x_k) \approx \frac{f_{k+1} - 2f_k + f_{k-1}}{\Delta x^2} . $$


The coefficient pattern $(1, -2, 1)/\Delta x^2$ is the discrete Laplacian; it reappears in every finite difference treatment of a diffusion equation, a beam equation or a Poisson problem.

2.4.2. Higher Order by Combining Stencils¶

Accuracy can be raised systematically by using more points. The central difference with step $\Delta x$ and the same formula with step $2\Delta x$ have known error expansions,


$$ D_0(\Delta x) = f' + \frac{\Delta x^2}{6}f''' + O(\Delta x^4), \qquad D_0(2\Delta x) = f' + \frac{4\Delta x^2}{6}f''' + O(\Delta x^4) . $$


The combination $\tfrac{1}{3}\bigl(4 D_0(\Delta x) - D_0(2\Delta x)\bigr)$ is built precisely so that the $\Delta x^2$ terms cancel, leaving


$$ f'(x) \approx \frac{-f(x + 2\Delta x) + 8f(x + \Delta x) - 8f(x - \Delta x) + f(x - 2\Delta x)}{12\,\Delta x} = f'(x) + O(\Delta x^4) . $$


This is the fourth-order central difference. Its five-point stencil uses four function evaluations instead of two, and by symmetry the next error term is $\Delta x^4$, not $\Delta x^3$. The same bookkeeping — write the Taylor expansion of each sample in the stencil, then choose the coefficients so that as many low-order terms as possible cancel — produces a finite difference formula for any derivative to any order of accuracy, and is how the coefficient tables in reference books are generated.

In [ ]:
dxs = np.logspace(-1, -5, 17)      # step sizes, from coarse to fine

# First Derivative, 3-point stencil
errC = np.abs((np.sin(x0 + dxs) - np.sin(x0 - dxs)) / (2 * dxs) - np.cos(x0))

# Second Derivative, 3-point stencil
err2 = np.abs((np.sin(x0 + dxs) - 2*np.sin(x0) + np.sin(x0 - dxs)) / dxs**2 + np.sin(x0))

# First Derivative, 5-point stencil
dfdx4 = (-np.sin(x0 + 2*dxs) + 8*np.sin(x0 + dxs)
         - 8*np.sin(x0 - dxs) + np.sin(x0 - 2*dxs)) / (12 * dxs)
err4 = np.abs(dfdx4 - np.cos(x0))

m = dxs > 1e-2                     # fit where truncation error dominates
print('second derivative, 3-point stencil : slope  %5.3f' % np.polyfit(np.log10(dxs[m]), np.log10(err2[m]), 1)[0])
print('first  derivative, 5-point stencil : slope  %5.3f' % np.polyfit(np.log10(dxs[m]), np.log10(err4[m]), 1)[0])

second derivative, 3-point stencil : slope  2.000
first  derivative, 5-point stencil : slope  3.999
In [ ]:
plt.loglog(dxs, errC, 'r^-', linewidth = 1.2)
plt.loglog(dxs, err4, 'md-', linewidth = 1.2)
plt.loglog(dxs, err2, 'cv-', linewidth = 1.2)
plt.legend(["$f'$,  3-point,  $O(\\Delta x^2)$", "$f'$,  5-point,  $O(\\Delta x^4)$",
            "$f''$,  3-point,  $O(\\Delta x^2)$"], fontsize = 12)
plt.grid(True, which = 'both')
plt.xlabel('$\\Delta x$', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('absolute error', fontsize = 12)
plt.show()

The measured slopes are $2.00$ and $4.00$. Two curves stop descending before the right edge of the plot: the fourth-order one bottoms out near $\Delta x \approx 5\times10^{-4}$, simply because it has already run out of digits to gain, and the second-derivative one near $\Delta x \approx 5\times10^{-5}$, because dividing by $\Delta x^2$ instead of $\Delta x$ amplifies roundoff far more aggressively.


2.5. Derivatives on a Grid¶

2.5.1. Interior Points and the Two Ends¶

In practice a function is rarely differentiated at one point. It is sampled on a grid


$$ x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n , \qquad x_k - x_{k-1} = \Delta x , \qquad f_k = f(x_k) , $$


and the whole array of derivatives is wanted at once. Here $\Delta x$ is no longer a free parameter — it is fixed by how densely the data were sampled.


The recipe follows directly from Sections 2.2 and 2.3. Use the central difference on the interior points $x_2, \dots, x_{n-1}$, where a neighbour exists on each side. At $x_1$ there is no point to the left, so use a forward difference; at $x_n$ there is no point to the right, so use a backward difference.


The sampled function is plotted first, with the sample points marked, as a reminder that the grid values are all the information available.

In [ ]:
n = 30
x = np.linspace(0.1, 3, n)
f = np.sin(x)

plt.plot(x, f, 'k')
plt.plot(x, f, 'rx', linewidth = 2)
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

print('grid spacing  dx = %.4f' % (x[1] - x[0]))

grid spacing  dx = 0.1000

The differencing itself is a three-line loop. Written this way it follows the recipe literally, one grid point at a time.

$$\frac{f(x_2) - f(x_1)}{\Delta x}$$


$$\frac{f(x_{k+1}) - f(x_{k-1})}{2 \Delta x}$$


$$\frac{f(x_n) - f(x_{n-1})}{\Delta x}$$

In [ ]:
dx = x[1] - x[0]
dfdx = np.zeros(n)

# Perform the finite differencing
dfdx[0] = (f[1] - f[0]) / (x[1] - x[0])                       # forward diff at f(x_1)
for i in range(1, n - 1):
    dfdx[i] = (f[i + 1] - f[i - 1]) / (x[i + 1] - x[i - 1])   # central in between
dfdx[-1] = (f[-1] - f[-2]) / (x[-1] - x[-2])                  # backward diff at f(x_n)
In [ ]:
plt.plot(x, np.cos(x), 'k', label = 'true derivative')
plt.plot(x, dfdx, 'rx', label = 'computed derivative')
plt.legend(fontsize = 12)
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

err = np.abs(dfdx - np.cos(x))
print('interior max error  %8.2e     predicted  dx^2/6         %8.2e' % (err[1:-1].max(), dx**2/6))
print('error at x_1        %8.2e     predicted  dx |f\'\'(x_1)|/2  %8.2e' % (err[0],  dx*abs(np.sin(x[0]))/2))
print('error at x_n        %8.2e     predicted  dx |f\'\'(x_n)|/2  %8.2e' % (err[-1], dx*abs(np.sin(x[-1]))/2))

interior max error  1.63e-03     predicted  dx^2/6         1.67e-03
error at x_1        6.65e-03     predicted  dx |f''(x_1)|/2  4.99e-03
error at x_n        8.70e-03     predicted  dx |f''(x_n)|/2  7.06e-03

The computed derivative follows $\cos x$ closely, and each printed error is within about $30\%$ of its predicted leading term — the rest is the next term of the expansion, which is not negligible at this coarse spacing. The two end points are about five times worse than the interior here, but the number five is not the point: the interior error is $O(\Delta x^2)$ and the end error is only $O(\Delta x)$, so the gap widens every time the grid is refined. The next cell measures that.


This is the single most common weakness of finite differences on a finite data record, and there are two standard cures. If the data are periodic, wrap around and use the central formula everywhere. Otherwise, use a second-order one-sided formula at the ends, built by the same Taylor bookkeeping as Section 2.4.2 but from the points that do exist:


$$ f'(x_1) \approx \frac{-3f_1 + 4f_2 - f_3}{2\Delta x} + O(\Delta x^2), \qquad f'(x_n) \approx \frac{3f_n - 4f_{n-1} + f_{n-2}}{2\Delta x} + O(\Delta x^2) . $$

In [ ]:
# how do the errors shrink as the grid is refined?
print('   n       dx     interior    ends, 1st order    ends, 2nd order')

for n in [30, 60, 120, 240]:
    x = np.linspace(0.1, 3, n)
    dx = x[1] - x[0]
    f = np.sin(x)

    # first-order ends, as above
    d1 = np.zeros(n)
    d1[0] = (f[1] - f[0]) / dx                                # forward diff at f(x_1)
    for i in range(1, n - 1):
        d1[i] = (f[i + 1] - f[i - 1]) / (2 * dx)              # central in between
    d1[-1] = (f[-1] - f[-2]) / dx                             # backward diff at f(x_n)

    # second-order ends, same interior
    d2 = d1.copy()
    d2[0] = (-3*f[0] + 4*f[1] - f[2]) / (2 * dx)
    d2[-1] = (3*f[-1] - 4*f[-2] + f[-3]) / (2 * dx)

    e1 = np.abs(d1 - np.cos(x))
    e2 = np.abs(d2 - np.cos(x))
    print('%4d  %7.4f   %8.2e         %8.2e           %8.2e'
          % (n, dx, e1[1:-1].max(), max(e1[0], e1[-1]), max(e2[0], e2[-1])))

   n       dx     interior    ends, 1st order    ends, 2nd order
  30   0.1000   1.63e-03         8.70e-03           3.28e-03
  60   0.0492   3.98e-04         3.87e-03           7.98e-04
 120   0.0244   9.82e-05         1.82e-03           1.97e-04
 240   0.0121   2.44e-05         8.80e-04           4.88e-05

Read the table down each column. Every time $n$ doubles, the interior error falls by a factor of $4$ and so does the second-order end error, while the first-order end error falls by only $2$. By $n = 240$ the cheap end formula is $36$ times worse than the interior, and it alone would decide the accuracy of anything built on top of these derivatives. The second-order ends stay within a factor of two of the interior at every resolution, which is what "matching the interior order" means in practice.


One remark on the code. The interior loop can be replaced by a single vectorized expression, in which the shifted arrays f[2:] and f[:-2] play the roles of $f_{k+1}$ and $f_{k-1}$ — for large grids this matters a great deal. NumPy packages the whole scheme as np.gradient, which uses central differences in the interior and, with edge_order = 2, the same one-sided formulas at the ends.

In [ ]:
n = 30
x = np.linspace(0.1, 3, n)
dx = x[1] - x[0]
f = np.sin(x)

# the same thing again, without the loop
dfdx = np.zeros(n)
dfdx[1:-1] = (f[2:] - f[:-2]) / (2 * dx)                      # central in between
dfdx[0] = (-3*f[0] + 4*f[1] - f[2]) / (2 * dx)                # 2nd-order forward
dfdx[-1] = (3*f[-1] - 4*f[-2] + f[-3]) / (2 * dx)             # 2nd-order backward

print('max difference from np.gradient  %8.1e' % np.max(np.abs(np.gradient(f, dx, edge_order = 2) - dfdx)))

max difference from np.gradient   2.2e-16




3. Numerical Integration¶

3.1. Why Numerical Integration?¶

3.1.1. Motivation¶

Most integrals that arise in engineering cannot be evaluated by the rules of calculus.

  • There is no antiderivative in closed form. Even innocent-looking integrands such as $e^{-x^2}$, $\sin(x)/x$ or $\sqrt{1 + \cos^2 x}$ (the arc length of a sine curve) have none.
  • The integrand is sampled data — a force record to be turned into an impulse, a flow rate to be turned into a volume, a power signal to be turned into energy. There is no formula to integrate at all.
  • The integrand is the output of a simulation or a black box, available one value at a time.

In each case the only thing we can do is evaluate $f$ at a finite set of points and combine those numbers into an estimate of the area. Every method below is of the form


$$ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \;\approx\; \sum_k w_k\,f(x_k) , $$


a weighted sum of samples. The methods differ only in where the points $x_k$ are placed and what the weights $w_k$ are.

3.1.2. The Riemann Sum¶

The definition of the integral is already a numerical method waiting to be used. Divide $[a, b]$ into $N$ equal pieces of width


$$ \Delta x = \frac{b - a}{N} , \qquad x_k = a + k\,\Delta x , \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, N , $$


so that $x_0 = a$ and $x_N = b$. Then


$$ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^{N} f\!\left(a + \frac{b-a}{N}k\right)\!\left(\frac{b-a}{N}\right) = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \sum_{k=1}^{N} f(x_k)\,\Delta x . $$


Each term $f(x_k)\,\Delta x$ is the area of a rectangle of width $\Delta x$ whose height is the value of $f$ at the right edge of the piece. Taking the height at the left edge instead gives the equally valid


$$ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} f(x_k)\,\Delta x . $$


As with the derivative, the numerical method is what is left when the limit is dropped and a finite $\Delta x$ is kept. The two choices of edge give the two rectangle rules of Section 3.2, and everything that follows is an attempt to do better than a rectangle.


Throughout we use the test integral


$$ \int_0^{10} \sin x \, dx = \bigl[-\cos x\bigr]_0^{10} = 1 - \cos 10 = 1.8390715\ldots , $$


whose exact value is known, so that every approximation can be compared with the truth.


3.2. Rectangle Rules¶

3.2.1. Left and Right Sums¶

Keeping $\Delta x$ finite in the two limits above gives the left-sided and right-sided rectangle rules,


$$ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \;\approx\; \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} f(x_k)\,\Delta x \qquad\text{and}\qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \;\approx\; \sum_{k=1}^{N} f(x_k)\,\Delta x . $$


Both are sums of $N$ rectangle areas; they differ only in which endpoint of each piece supplies the height. Note that each uses $N$ of the $N+1$ available samples, the left rule ignoring $f(b)$ and the right rule ignoring $f(a)$.


We take $a = 0$, $b = 10$, $\Delta x = 0.5$, and sample $\sin x$ on that grid. The dashed line in the plot is the staircase whose area the left-sided rule computes.

In [ ]:
a = 0
b = 10

dx = 0.5
x = np.arange(a, b + dx, dx)
fx = np.sin(x)

n = len(x)                 # number of data points
print('number of data points  n =', n)
print('number of rectangles   N =', n - 1)

exact = 1 - np.cos(10)     # the value we are trying to reproduce
print('exact integral          ', exact)

number of data points  n = 21
number of rectangles   N = 20
exact integral           1.8390715290764525
In [ ]:
# Plot
plt.plot(x, fx, '-k', linewidth = 2)
plt.step(x, fx, '--r', where = 'post')      # the staircase of the left-sided rule
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('$x$', fontsize = 12)
plt.show()

The picture below shows the two sets of rectangles themselves. Where $f$ is increasing the left rectangles sit below the curve and the right rectangles above it; where $f$ is decreasing the roles are reversed. That observation is the whole story of the error.

In [ ]:
xf = np.linspace(a, b, 400)

plt.figure(figsize = (13, 3.6))

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.bar(x[:-1], fx[:-1], width = dx, align = 'edge', color = 'c', edgecolor = 'k', linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.5)
plt.plot(xf, np.sin(xf), '-k', linewidth = 2)
# plt.grid(True)
plt.xlim([0, 10])
plt.title('left-sided rectangles')

plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.bar(x[:-1], fx[1:], width = dx, align = 'edge', color = 'y', edgecolor = 'k', linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.5)
plt.plot(xf, np.sin(xf), '-k', linewidth = 2)
plt.xlim([0, 10])
# plt.grid(True)
plt.title('right-sided rectangles')
plt.show()

The two sums are written below exactly as they read: add one rectangle area at a time.

In [ ]:
# left-sided rectangle rule
areaL = 0
for i in range(n - 1):
    areaL = areaL + fx[i]*dx

# right-sided rectangle rule
areaR = 0
for i in range(n - 1):
    areaR = areaR + fx[i + 1]*dx

print('areaL  %10.6f    error %+9.6f' % (areaL, areaL - exact))
print('areaR  %10.6f    error %+9.6f' % (areaR, areaR - exact))

areaL    1.936602    error +0.097531
areaR    1.664592    error -0.174480

A loop is the clearest way to write a sum once, but NumPy can add the whole array at a stroke. The left rule adds the first $N$ samples, the right rule the last $N$, and both multiply by $\Delta x$.

In [ ]:
# the same two sums, without the loop
areaL = np.sum(fx[:-1])*dx
areaR = np.sum(fx[1:])*dx

print('areaL  %10.6f' % areaL)
print('areaR  %10.6f' % areaR)

print('\nareaR - areaL           %+9.6f' % (areaR - areaL))
print('( f(b) - f(a) ) * dx    %+9.6f' % ((fx[-1] - fx[0])*dx))

areaL    1.936602
areaR    1.664592

areaR - areaL           -0.272011
( f(b) - f(a) ) * dx    -0.272011

3.2.2. Why the Rectangle Rules Are First Order¶

The two sums differ by $0.272$, which is a large disagreement for two approximations of the same number. The last check explains it exactly. The two sums contain the same interior samples $f(x_1), \dots, f(x_{N-1})$; only the two ends differ, so


$$ \text{areaR} - \text{areaL} = \bigl(f(b) - f(a)\bigr)\,\Delta x , $$


which the code confirms to the last digit. The difference shrinks like $\Delta x$, and neither sum is closer to the truth than that difference — so both must carry an error of order $\Delta x$.


The same conclusion follows from a Taylor expansion on one piece. With $x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta x$,


$$ \int_{x_k}^{x_{k+1}} f(x)\,dx = \Delta x\, f(x_k) + \frac{\Delta x^2}{2}f'(x_k) + O(\Delta x^3) , $$


so a single left rectangle misses by $\tfrac{\Delta x^2}{2}f'(x_k)$. Summing over all $N$ pieces, and recognizing $\Delta x\sum f'(x_k)$ as a Riemann sum for $\int f'$,


$$ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx - \text{areaL} \;\approx\; \frac{\Delta x}{2}\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = \frac{\Delta x}{2}\bigl(f(b) - f(a)\bigr) . $$


The error of a single rectangle is $O(\Delta x^2)$, but there are $N \propto 1/\Delta x$ of them, so the total error is $O(\Delta x)$ — first-order accurate. Halving $\Delta x$ only halves the error. The right rule has the same error with the opposite sign, which is exactly what the next section exploits.


3.3. The Trapezoidal Rule¶

3.3.1. Averaging the Two Rectangles¶

The left rule misses by $+\tfrac{\Delta x}{2}(f(b) - f(a))$ and the right rule by $-\tfrac{\Delta x}{2}(f(b) - f(a))$. Averaging them must cancel that term. Geometrically, replacing each rectangle by the average of the left and right rectangle is the same as joining $(x_k, f_k)$ to $(x_{k+1}, f_{k+1})$ by a straight line: the shape becomes a trapezoid of area $\tfrac{\Delta x}{2}(f_k + f_{k+1})$, and the rule is


$$ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \;\approx\; \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \frac{\Delta x}{2}\bigl(f_k + f_{k+1}\bigr) . $$


Collecting terms, every interior sample appears in two trapezoids and the two end samples in one each, so the rule can also be written with explicit weights,


$$ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \;\approx\; \Delta x\left(\frac{f_0}{2} + f_1 + f_2 + \cdots + f_{N-1} + \frac{f_N}{2}\right) . $$


The trapezoidal rule therefore costs nothing beyond the rectangle rules: it uses the same $N + 1$ samples and only weights the two ends by one half.

In [ ]:
# trapezoidal rule
Z = 0
for i in range(n - 1):
    Z = Z + (dx/2)*(fx[i + 1] + fx[i])

print('areaZ  %10.6f    error %+9.6f' % (Z, Z - exact))

# it really is the average of the two rectangle rules
print('\n(areaL + areaR) / 2     %10.6f' % ((areaL + areaR)/2))

# and NumPy has it built in
print('np.trapezoid(fx, x)     %10.6f' % np.trapezoid(fx, x))

areaZ    1.800597    error -0.038475

(areaL + areaR) / 2       1.800597
np.trapezoid(fx, x)       1.800597

The three numbers agree exactly. NumPy's np.trapezoid is the direct counterpart of MATLAB's trapz, and it takes the sampled values and the sample points, so it works on measured data just as well as on a formula. (In NumPy versions before $2.0$ the same function is called np.trapz.)

In [ ]:
a = 0
b = 10

dx = 0.5
x = np.arange(a, b + dx, dx)
fx = np.sin(x)

n = len(x)                 # number of data points
print('number of data points  n =', n)
print('number of trapezoids    N =', n - 1)

exact = 1 - np.cos(10)     # the exact value
print('exact integral          ', exact)

# Trapezoidal Rule
integral = np.sum((fx[:-1] + fx[1:]) * dx / 2)

print('trapezoidal integral    ', integral)
print('absolute error           ', abs(integral - exact))

xf = np.linspace(a, b, 400)

plt.figure(figsize = (13, 3.6))

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)

# Plot the trapezoids
for i in range(n - 1):
    x_trap = [x[i], x[i], x[i+1], x[i+1]]
    y_trap = [0, fx[i], fx[i+1], 0]

    plt.fill(x_trap, y_trap, color = 'b', alpha = 0.5)
    plt.plot([x[i], x[i+1]], [fx[i], fx[i+1]], 'k-', linewidth = 1)

# Exact function
plt.plot(xf, np.sin(xf), '-k', linewidth = 2)

plt.xlim([0, 10])
plt.title('Trapezoidal Rule')

plt.show()

number of data points  n = 21
number of trapezoids    N = 20
exact integral           1.8390715290764525
trapezoidal integral     1.8005969410370184
absolute error            0.038474588039434154

3.3.2. Why the Trapezoidal Rule Is Second Order¶

The error of the trapezoidal rule on the whole interval is


$$ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx - \text{areaZ} \;=\; -\frac{\Delta x^2}{12}\bigl(f'(b) - f'(a)\bigr) + O(\Delta x^4) , $$


so it is second-order accurate: halving $\Delta x$ divides the error by four. The cancellation of the first-order term is the same phenomenon met in Chapter 2, where averaging the forward and backward differences produced the second-order central difference. Symmetry buys an order of accuracy, and it is free.


The formula also predicts the error, not just its order, and at $\Delta x = 0.5$ it does so to three digits.

In [ ]:
print('actual error       %+9.6f' % (Z - exact))
print('predicted error    %+9.6f' % (dx**2/12*(np.cos(10) - np.cos(0))))

actual error       -0.038475
predicted error    -0.038314

Remark (when the trapezoidal rule is extraordinary). The error depends only on the derivatives at the two endpoints. If $f$ is smooth and periodic and $[a, b]$ spans a whole number of periods, then $f'(b) = f'(a)$, every term of the expansion cancels, and the trapezoidal rule converges faster than any power of $\Delta x$. This is why simple equally-spaced sums are the method of choice for periodic problems, and it is the basis of spectral methods.


Every rule so far has placed its sample points on a grid, and every one has become more accurate as that grid was refined. The last section of this chapter abandons the grid altogether.


3.4. Monte Carlo Integration¶

3.4.1. Sampling Instead of a Grid¶

Monte Carlo integration is a class of algorithms that rely on repeated random sampling to obtain a numerical result. Unlike the rules of Sections 3.2 and 3.3, which evaluate the integrand at fixed, equally spaced points, a Monte Carlo method evaluates it at points drawn at random from the domain of integration.


Named after the casino in Monaco, these methods were developed in the 1940s by Stanislaw Ulam, John von Neumann and Nicholas Metropolis as part of the Manhattan Project. They are now indispensable in physics, financial engineering, statistical mechanics and machine learning.


The formulation begins with the integral of a continuous function $f$ over a domain $\Omega = [a, b]$ whose total length is $|\Omega| = b - a$,


$$ I = \int_{\Omega} f(x)\,dx . $$


If $X$ is a random variable drawn uniformly from $\Omega$, its probability density is the constant $p(x) = 1/|\Omega|$, and the integral can be rewritten as an expected value:


$$ I = |\Omega| \int_{\Omega} f(x)\,\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\,dx = |\Omega| \cdot \mathbb{E}[f(X)] . $$


An expected value is approximated by a sample mean. Drawing $N$ independent points $x_1, \dots, x_N$ uniformly from $\Omega$ gives the Monte Carlo estimate


$$ \int_{\Omega} f(x)\,dx \;\approx\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} f(x_j)\,|\Omega| , \qquad x_j \sim \mathcal{U}(\Omega) . $$


This is still the weighted sum of samples introduced in Section 3.1.1, $\sum_k w_k f(x_k)$. What has changed is that the points are no longer chosen and the weights are all equal to $|\Omega|/N$. Read geometrically, each sample defines a rectangle of width $b - a$ and height $f(x_j)$, and the estimate is the average area of $N$ such rectangles. With $N = 4$,


$$ I \approx \frac{1}{4}\Bigl[ f(x_1)(b-a) + f(x_2)(b-a) + f(x_3)(b-a) + f(x_4)(b-a) \Bigr] , $$


and as $N \to \infty$ the average area of these stochastic rectangles converges to the exact area under the curve.

3.4.2. Hit-or-Miss: the Area of a Circle¶

There is a second, even more elementary way to see the idea, and it applies to a region rather than to a function. Let $\Omega$ be a domain of unknown area $A$, contained in a simple bounding region $B$ whose area $A_B$ is known. If $N$ points are scattered uniformly over $B$, the probability that any one of them lands in $\Omega$ is the ratio of the areas,


$$ P = \frac{\text{Area}(\Omega)}{\text{Area}(B)} = \frac{A}{A_B} . $$


By the law of large numbers, the observed fraction converges to that probability as $N$ grows, so with $N_{\text{inside}}$ points landing in $\Omega$,


$$ \frac{N_{\text{inside}}}{N} \approx \frac{A}{A_B} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad A \approx A_B \cdot \frac{N_{\text{inside}}}{N} . $$


This is the hit-or-miss technique. As a demonstration we estimate the area of the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 \le 1$, whose exact value is $\pi$, by enclosing it in the square $[-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]$:

  1. Define the bounding box. The square has area $A_{\text{box}} = 2 \times 2 = 4$.
  2. Generate samples. Draw $N$ independent uniform points $(x_i, y_i)$ from $[-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]$.
  3. Inclusion test. Check whether $x_i^2 + y_i^2 \le 1$.
  4. Compute the estimate. Take $A \approx 4 \cdot N_{\text{inside}}/N$, and plot a subset of the points to see the sampling distribution inside and outside the boundary.
In [ ]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)

# 1. Setup Parameters
n_samples = 1000000
box_area = 4.0

# 2. Generate Random Points
x = np.random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0, n_samples)
y = np.random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0, n_samples)

# 3. Check Points Inside Circle
distance_squared = x**2 + y**2
inside_mask = distance_squared <= 1.0
n_inside = np.sum(inside_mask)

# 4. Calculate Estimated Area
estimated_area = box_area * (n_inside / n_samples)
exact_area = np.pi
error_percent = abs(estimated_area - exact_area) / exact_area * 100

# 5. Display Results
print(f"Total Samples: {n_samples:,}")
print('Estimated Area: %.5f' % estimated_area)
print('Exact Area (Pi): %.5f' % exact_area)
print('Error: %.3f%%' % error_percent)

# 6. Plot Sample Points (Subset of 5,000 points for clarity)
n_plot = 2000
plt.figure(figsize = (6, 6))
plt.scatter(x[:n_plot][inside_mask[:n_plot]], y[:n_plot][inside_mask[:n_plot]], color = 'crimson', s = 2, label = 'Inside')
plt.scatter(x[:n_plot][~inside_mask[:n_plot]], y[:n_plot][~inside_mask[:n_plot]], color = 'royalblue', s = 2, label = 'Outside')

# Boundary Circle
theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
plt.plot(np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta), 'k--', linewidth = 1.5, label = 'Boundary')

plt.xlim(-1, 1)
plt.ylim(-1, 1)
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal')
plt.title('Monte Carlo Integration: Unit Circle Area')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('y')
plt.legend(loc = 'upper right')
plt.grid(True, linestyle = ':', alpha = 0.5)
plt.show()

Total Samples: 1,000,000
Estimated Area: 3.14169
Exact Area (Pi): 3.14159
Error: 0.003%

A million samples locate $\pi$ to three decimal places. That is a modest return for so much arithmetic, and the reason is the subject of Section 3.4.4.

3.4.3. Sample Mean: a One-Dimensional Integral¶

The expected-value formulation of Section 3.4.1 is applied next to a definite integral,


$$ I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \bigl( \sin x + 0.5\cos 3x + 1 \bigr)\,dx . $$


  1. Analytical solution. $\displaystyle I_{\text{exact}} = \Bigl[-\cos x + \tfrac{1}{6}\sin 3x + x\Bigr]_0^{\pi} = 2 + \pi \approx 5.14159$.
  2. Domain length. $|\Omega| = b - a = \pi$.
  3. Computation. The integrand and the area to be computed are plotted first; then $N$ points $x_i \sim \mathcal{U}(0, \pi)$ are drawn and the integral is estimated as the mean height times the domain length.
In [ ]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Setup Function and Domain [0, pi]
a, b = 0.0, np.pi
x_plot = np.linspace(a, b, 500)
# f(x) = sin(x) + 0.5*cos(3x) + 1.0
fx_plot = np.sin(x_plot) + 0.5 * np.cos(3 * x_plot) + 1.0

# 2. Plot Function Curve
plt.figure(figsize = (6, 4))
plt.plot(x_plot, fx_plot, 'b-', linewidth = 2, label = r'$f(x) = \sin(x) + 0.5\cos(3x) + 1.0$')

# 3. Fill Integration Area [0, pi]
plt.fill_between(x_plot, fx_plot, color = 'skyblue', alpha = 0.4, label = 'Integration Area')

# 4. Display Settings
plt.axhline(0, color = 'black', linewidth = 0.8, linestyle = '--')
plt.axvline(a, color = 'gray', linestyle = '--')
plt.axvline(b, color = 'gray', linestyle = '--')
plt.title(r'Integrand Function $f(x)$ over $[0, \pi]$')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('f(x)')
plt.grid(True, linestyle = ':', alpha = 0.6)
# plt.legend(loc='upper right')
plt.show()
In [ ]:
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(0)

# 1. Setup Domain and Parameters
a, b = 0.0, np.pi
domain_length = b - a
n_samples = 1000000

# 2. Generate Uniform Random Samples
x = np.random.uniform(a, b, n_samples)

# 3. Evaluate Integrand: f(x) = sin(x) + 0.5*cos(3x) + 1.0
fx = np.sin(x) + 0.5 * np.cos(3 * x) + 1.0

# 4. Compute Monte Carlo Estimate (Domain Length * Mean Height)
estimated_integral = domain_length * np.mean(fx)

# Analytical exact value: [-cos(x) + (1/6)*sin(3x) + 1.0x] from 0 to pi = 2 + pi approx 5.14159
exact_integral = 2.0 + np.pi
error_percent = abs(estimated_integral - exact_integral) / exact_integral * 100

# 5. Display Results
print(f"Total Samples: {n_samples:,}")
print('Estimated Integral: %.5f' % estimated_integral)
print('Exact Integral: %.5f' % exact_integral)
print('Error: %.3f%%' % error_percent)

Total Samples: 1,000,000
Estimated Integral: 5.14153
Exact Integral: 5.14159
Error: 0.001%

There is no grid anywhere in that computation, and no formula for weights: the entire method is "evaluate $f$ at random points and average". Nothing in it refers to the dimension of the domain either, which is the property that matters next.

3.4.4. Convergence and the Curse of Dimensionality¶

The estimate is itself a random variable, so a different set of samples gives a different answer. By the central limit theorem its standard deviation is


$$ \text{Error} = \mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\right) , $$


which is a discouraging rate: to gain one more decimal digit, $N$ must be multiplied by one hundred. It is far worse than the $O(\Delta x^2)$ of the trapezoidal rule. Section 3.4.3 showed exactly that: the million random points used there reach a relative error of about $10^{-5}$, which the trapezoidal rule attains on the same integral with about one hundred and sixty subintervals.


The crucial property is not the rate itself but what the rate does not depend on. The exponent $1/2$ is the same in one dimension and in one thousand, because it comes from the statistics of averaging and not from the geometry of a grid.


A grid-based rule has no such immunity. Covering a $d$-dimensional cube with $n$ points per side requires $N = n^d$ evaluations in total, so the spacing is $\Delta x \sim n^{-1} = N^{-1/d}$ and the trapezoidal error $O(\Delta x^2)$ becomes


$$ \mathcal{O}\bigl(N^{-2/d}\bigr) . $$


The comparison is then immediate. In one dimension $N^{-2}$ is vastly better than $N^{-1/2}$, and a grid should be used. The two rates coincide at $d = 4$, and beyond that the grid rule falls behind and keeps falling: at $d = 10$ its error decays as $N^{-1/5}$ while the Monte Carlo error still decays as $N^{-1/2}$. This deterioration of grid methods with dimension is the curse of dimensionality, and escaping it is the reason Monte Carlo integration is used at all.


Remark (where high-dimensional integrals come from). Ten dimensions is not an exotic case. An expected value over a system with ten uncertain parameters, a partition function in statistical mechanics, the price of an option depending on many correlated assets, and the expected loss of a machine learning model over its data distribution are all integrals whose dimension is the number of variables in the problem. For these, sampling is not one option among several; it is the only one.




4. Numerical Solutions to ODEs¶

4.1. From Integration to Differential Equations¶

4.1.1. The Initial Value Problem¶

Almost every dynamical model in engineering can be written as a first-order system


$$ \dot{x} = f(x) , \qquad x(0) = x_0 , $$


where $x$ may be a vector of states and $f$ may be a nonlinear function. A second-order equation is put in this form by naming the velocity as an extra state, as Sections 4.2 and 4.5 will do.


The special case in which $f$ is linear,


$$ \dot{x} = A x , \qquad x(0) = x_0 , $$


is a system of first-order linear differential equations, and it has the closed-form solution $x(t) = e^{At}x_0$. That solution is the exception: for a general nonlinear $f$ no formula exists, and we must compute instead.


What "compute" means here is worth stating precisely. A numerical solver does not return a function. Starting from $x_0$ it iterates, producing


$$ x_0 \;\to\; x_1 \;\to\; x_2 \;\to\; \cdots \;\to\; x_N , \qquad x_k \approx x(t_k), \qquad t_k = k\,\Delta t , $$


a finite list of states sampled along the solution. That list is called a trajectory. Every method in this chapter is a rule for getting from $x_k$ to $x_{k+1}$.

4.1.2. Forward and Backward Euler¶

The simplest rules come straight from the finite differences of two sections ago. Replace $\dot{x}$ by a forward difference and evaluate the right-hand side at the point we already know:


$$ \frac{x_{k+1} - x_k}{\Delta t} \approx \dot{x} = f(x_k) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \;x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta t\, f(x_k)\; $$


This is forward Euler, also called the explicit Euler method. Everything on the right is known, so the new state is obtained by one evaluation of $f$ and one addition. Geometrically it is the tangent line: follow the slope at the current point for one step.


Replacing $\dot{x}$ by a backward difference instead evaluates the right-hand side at the point we are trying to find:


$$ \frac{x_{k+1} - x_k}{\Delta t} \approx \dot x = f(x_{k+1}) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \;x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta t\, f(x_{k+1}) $$


This is backward Euler, or the implicit Euler method. The unknown $x_{k+1}$ now appears on both sides, so each step requires solving an equation rather than evaluating a formula. For a general nonlinear $f$ that means a rootfinding problem at every step — which is where Newton's method earns its keep. Section 4.4 explains why anyone would pay that price.


For a linear system the implicit equation can be solved once and for all. With $f(x) = Ax$,


$$ \text{forward:}\quad x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta t\, A x_k = \bigl(I + \Delta t A\bigr)x_k , $$

$$ \text{backward:}\quad x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta t\, A x_{k+1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_{k+1} = \bigl(I - \Delta t A\bigr)^{-1} x_k , $$


where $I$ is the identity matrix. Both are just a matrix multiplied by the current state; the difference is which matrix.


4.2. A Linear Example: the Spring-Mass-Damper¶

4.2.1. The Model¶

A mass $m$ on a spring of stiffness $K$ with a damper of constant $c$ obeys


$$ m\ddot{x} = -Kx - c\dot{x} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \ddot{x} + \frac{c}{m}\dot{x} + \frac{K}{m}x = 0 . $$


Introducing the natural frequency and the damping ratio


$$ \omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{K}{m}} , \qquad \zeta = \frac{c}{2\sqrt{Km}} , $$


puts it in the standard form of a second-order linear differential equation,


$$ \ddot{x} + 2\zeta\omega_0\dot{x} + \omega_0^2 x = 0 . $$


To solve it numerically we need a first-order system, so we name the velocity $v = \dot{x}$ as a second state:


$$ \begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= v \\ \dot{v} &= -\omega_0^2 x - 2\zeta\omega_0 v \end{aligned} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ v \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -\omega_0^2 & -2\zeta\omega_0 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ v \end{bmatrix} . $$


This trick — adding the derivative as a state — turns any $n$-th order equation into a first-order system of $n$ equations, which is why solvers only ever need to handle the form $\dot{x} = f(x)$.


The two numbers $\omega_0$ and $\zeta$ fix the eigenvalues of $A$, and therefore the entire behaviour:

  • under-damped, $\zeta < 1$: the system oscillates while decaying, at the damped frequency $\omega_d = \omega_0\sqrt{1 - \zeta^2}$;
  • critically damped, $\zeta = 1$: the fastest decay without oscillation;
  • over-damped, $\zeta > 1$: two real decay rates, no oscillation.

We take $\omega_0 = 2\pi$ (a one-second period) and $\zeta = 1.75$, an over-damped case, released from rest at $x = 2$.

In [ ]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

w = 2*np.pi
d = 1.75            # damping ratio (zeta)

A = np.array([[0, 1], [-w**2, -2*d*w]])

dt = 0.1            # time step
T = 5              # amount of time to integrate

x0 = np.array([2, 0])     # initial condition

print('A =\n', A)
print('\neigenvalues of A ', np.linalg.eigvals(A))

A =
 [[  0.           1.        ]
 [-39.4784176  -21.99114858]]

eigenvalues of A  [ -1.97203638 -20.01911219]

Both eigenvalues are real and negative, confirming the over-damped case, and the true solution decays to zero. Note how different their sizes are: one mode decays on a time scale of $1/2$ second, the other about ten times faster. Remember that gap; Section 4.4 shows that it is what limits the step size.

4.2.2. Coding the Two Euler Methods¶

Each method is a loop over the same three lines: start from $x_0$, apply the update rule, store the result. For this linear system the update is a single matrix multiplication, so the matrix is formed once outside the loop.

In [ ]:
n = int(T/dt)       # number of steps

# iterate forward Euler
xF = np.zeros((2, n + 1))
tF = np.zeros(n + 1)
xF[:, 0] = x0
for i in range(n):
    tF[i + 1] = (i + 1)*dt
    xF[:, i + 1] = (np.eye(2) + A*dt) @ xF[:, i]

# iterate backward Euler
xB = np.zeros((2, n + 1))
tB = np.zeros(n + 1)
xB[:, 0] = x0
for i in range(n):
    tB[i + 1] = (i + 1)*dt
    xB[:, i + 1] = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(2) - A*dt) @ xB[:, i]

# compute better solution using a built-in solver
sol = solve_ivp(lambda t, y: A @ y, (0, T), x0, t_eval = np.arange(0, T + dt, dt))
t = sol.t
y = sol.y
In [ ]:
plt.plot(tB, xB[0, :], 'w')      # backward euler
plt.plot(tF, xF[0, :], 'y', label = 'Forward Euler')      # forward euler



plt.plot(t, y[0, :], 'k--', label = 'Ground Truth')        # built-in solver
# plt.legend(['Forward Euler', 'Backward Euler', 'solve_ivp'], fontsize=12)
plt.legend()
# plt.grid(True)
plt.xlim([0, T])
plt.xlabel('$t$', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('$x$', fontsize = 12)
plt.title('$\\Delta t = %g$' % dt, fontsize = 12)
plt.show()

print('x at t = T')
print('   Forward Euler   %10.4f' % xF[0, -1])
print('   Backward Euler  %10.4f' % xB[0, -1])
print('   solve_ivp       %10.4f' % y[0, -1])

x at t = T
   Forward Euler      -0.2404
   Backward Euler      0.0003
   solve_ivp           0.0001

Something is wrong. The true solution has decayed to essentially zero by $t = 5$, and backward Euler and the library solver agree that it has — but forward Euler is still oscillating with an amplitude of about $0.24$, and if the plot is continued the oscillation grows. It is not merely inaccurate; it is qualitatively wrong, producing oscillation in a system that cannot oscillate.


The obvious first response is to shrink the step. It works, and the reason it works is the subject of Section 4.4.

In [ ]:
plt.plot(tF, xF[0, :], 'w')      # forward euler

dt = 0.05           # half as large
n = int(T/dt)

xF = np.zeros((2, n + 1))
tF = np.arange(n + 1)*dt
xF[:, 0] = x0
for i in range(n):
    xF[:, i + 1] = (np.eye(2) + A*dt) @ xF[:, i]

xB = np.zeros((2, n + 1))
xB[:, 0] = x0
for i in range(n):
    xB[:, i + 1] = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(2) - A*dt) @ xB[:, i]

sol = solve_ivp(lambda t, y: A @ y, (0, T), x0, t_eval = tF)

# plt.plot(tF, xB[0, :], 'w')
plt.plot(tF, xF[0, :], 'y', label = 'Forward Euler')

plt.plot(sol.t, sol.y[0, :], 'k--', label = 'Ground Truth')
# plt.legend(['Forward Euler', 'Backward Euler', 'solve_ivp'], fontsize=12)
# plt.grid(True)
plt.xlim([0, T])
plt.ylabel('$x$', fontsize = 12)
plt.legend()
plt.xlabel('$t$', fontsize = 12)
plt.title('$\\Delta t = %g$' % dt, fontsize = 12)
plt.show()

print('x at t = T   Forward %10.3e   Backward %10.3e   solve_ivp %10.3e'
      % (xF[0, -1], xB[0, -1], sol.y[0, -1]))

x at t = T   Forward  6.882e-05   Backward  1.828e-04   solve_ivp  1.158e-04

With $\Delta t = 0.05$ all three results agree to about $10^{-4}$ and decay to zero. The step size mattered far more than the choice of method.


4.3. Error¶

4.3.1. Local and Global Error¶

How wrong is one Euler step? Write the scalar case $\dot{y} = f(y)$ and expand the exact solution about $t_k$:


$$ y(t_k + \Delta t) = y(t_k) + \Delta t\,\frac{dy}{dt}(t_k) + \frac{\Delta t^2}{2!}\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}(c) , \qquad c \in [t_k, t_{k+1}] , $$


where the last term is the exact Taylor remainder. Since $\dot{y}(t_k) = f(y_k)$, the first two terms are exactly the forward Euler step. Everything the method throws away is the third term, so the local error — the error committed by one step, starting from an exact value — is


$$ \epsilon_{k+1} = y(t_k + \Delta t) - y_{k+1} = \frac{\Delta t^2}{2}\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}(c) = O(\Delta t^2) . $$


That looks encouraging, but it is not the number we care about. Reaching a fixed final time $b$ from $a$ takes $N = (b-a)/\Delta t$ steps, and the local errors accumulate. Adding them up gives the global error


$$ E_N = \sum_{k} \epsilon_k \;\approx\; N \cdot \frac{\Delta t^2}{2}\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} = \frac{b-a}{2}\,\Delta t\,\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} = O(\Delta t) . $$


One power of $\Delta t$ is lost to the number of steps. Forward Euler is therefore a first-order method: halving the step size halves the error at the final time. Backward Euler has the same structure with the opposite sign on its remainder, and is also first order.


Remark (this is the same bookkeeping as the rectangle rule). In Chapter 3 a single rectangle had an $O(\Delta x^2)$ error, there were $N \propto 1/\Delta x$ of them, and the total was $O(\Delta x)$. That is not a coincidence: applying forward Euler to the special case $\dot{y} = f(t)$ is the left-rectangle rule, and backward Euler is the right-rectangle rule. The trapezoidal rule has a differential-equation counterpart too — averaging the two slopes gives $x_{k+1} = x_k + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\bigl(f(x_k) + f(x_{k+1})\bigr)$, the second-order Crank-Nicolson method.

4.3.2. Measuring the Order¶

The claim is checked as always: halve the step and watch the error at a fixed final time. We compare against the exact solution $x(T) = e^{AT}x_0$, which for this linear system can be computed to machine precision.

In [ ]:
T = 1.0
exact = expm(A*T) @ x0
print('exact x(T) = %.8f\n' % exact[0])

print('     dt        FE error     ratio      BE error     ratio')

eF_old = eB_old = 0

for dt in [0.05, 0.025, 0.0125, 0.00625, 0.003125]:
    n = int(round(T/dt))

    xF = x0.astype(float)
    xB = x0.astype(float)
    MF = np.eye(2) + A*dt
    MB = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(2) - A*dt)
    for i in range(n):
        xF = MF @ xF
        xB = MB @ xB

    eF = abs(xF[0] - exact[0])
    eB = abs(xB[0] - exact[0])

    if eF_old == 0:
        print('%9.6f  %10.3e       -     %10.3e       -' % (dt, eF, eB))
    else:
        print('%9.6f  %10.3e   %6.2f    %10.3e   %6.2f' % (dt, eF, eF_old/eF, eB, eB_old/eB))

    eF_old, eB_old = eF, eB

exact x(T) = 0.30876172

     dt        FE error     ratio      BE error     ratio
 0.050000   3.053e-02       -      2.951e-02       -
 0.025000   1.514e-02     2.02     1.488e-02     1.98
 0.012500   7.537e-03     2.01     7.473e-03     1.99
 0.006250   3.760e-03     2.00     3.744e-03     2.00
 0.003125   1.878e-03     2.00     1.874e-03     2.00

Both ratios settle on $2$: halving $\Delta t$ halves the error, which is first-order convergence. The two methods are almost equally accurate — their error constants differ by only a few percent. Accuracy is not the reason to prefer one over the other.


4.4. Stability¶

4.4.1. The Scalar Test Problem¶

Accuracy asks how far a method drifts from the truth over a fixed interval. Stability asks something cruder and more urgent: does the computed solution stay bounded at all? The failure in Section 4.2.2 was a stability failure, and one scalar problem explains it completely.


Take


$$ \dot{y} = \lambda y , \qquad y(0) = y_0 , $$


whose exact solution $y(t) = e^{\lambda t}y_0$ decays whenever $\operatorname{Re}\lambda < 0$. The two methods give


$$ \text{forward:}\quad y_{k+1} = (1 + \lambda\Delta t)\,y_k , \qquad \text{backward:}\quad y_{k+1} = \frac{1}{1 - \lambda\Delta t}\,y_k . $$


Each step multiplies by a fixed number, so after $N$ steps


$$ y_N = (1 + \lambda\Delta t)^N y_0 , \qquad y_N = \left(\frac{1}{1 - \lambda\Delta t}\right)^{\!N} y_0 . $$


A power $g^N$ stays bounded exactly when $|g| \le 1$. The two methods are therefore unstable when


$$ \bigl|1 + \lambda\Delta t\bigr| > 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \left|\frac{1}{1 - \lambda\Delta t}\right| > 1 . $$


Write $z = \lambda\Delta t$, a complex number combining the physics ($\lambda$) with our choice ($\Delta t$). Forward Euler is stable for $|1 + z| \le 1$: a disc of radius one centred at $z = -1$. Backward Euler is stable for $|1 - z| \ge 1$: everything outside the disc of radius one centred at $z = +1$ — which includes the entire left half-plane.


That is the whole story. If the true solution decays, backward Euler will decay too, whatever step size is chosen. Forward Euler will only decay if $\lambda\Delta t$ happens to land in its small disc. For a real negative $\lambda$ the condition reduces to


$$ \Delta t \le \frac{2}{|\lambda|} , $$


a hard ceiling set by the fastest decaying mode in the problem, however uninteresting that mode may be.

In [ ]:
# the two stability regions in the complex plane  z = lambda*dt
re = np.linspace(-3, 3, 400)
im = np.linspace(-3, 3, 400)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(re, im)
Z = X + 1j*Y

plt.figure(figsize = (11, 4.5))

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.contourf(X, Y, np.abs(1 + Z), levels = [0, 1], colors = ['c'])
plt.axhline(0, color = 'k', linewidth = 0.5)
plt.axvline(0, color = 'k', linewidth = 0.5)
plt.grid(True)
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal', adjustable = 'box')
plt.xlabel('Re $z$', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('Im $z$', fontsize = 12)
plt.title('Forward Euler:  stable where $|1 + z| \\leq 1$', fontsize = 11)

plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.contourf(X, Y, np.abs(1/(1 - Z)), levels = [0, 1], colors = ['c'])
plt.axhline(0, color = 'k', linewidth = 0.5)
plt.axvline(0, color = 'k', linewidth = 0.5)
plt.grid(True)
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal', adjustable = 'box')
plt.xlabel('Re $z$', fontsize = 12)
plt.title('Backward Euler:  stable where $|1 - z| \\geq 1$', fontsize = 11)
plt.show()

The shaded regions are where each method is stable. Forward Euler owns one small disc; backward Euler owns everything except one small disc, and in particular the whole left half-plane where all decaying physics lives. This is what "better stability" means, and it is the reason for tolerating the cost of solving an equation at every step.

4.4.2. Systems: the Eigenvalue Test¶

For a system $\dot{x} = Ax$ the same argument applies to each mode. After $N$ steps,


$$ x_N = \bigl(I + \Delta t A\bigr)^{N} x_0 , \qquad x_N = \bigl(I - \Delta t A\bigr)^{-N} x_0 , $$


and a matrix power stays bounded exactly when every eigenvalue of that matrix has magnitude at most one. So


$$ \text{forward Euler is stable when } \bigl|\text{eig}\bigl(I + \Delta t A\bigr)\bigr| \le 1 , \qquad \text{backward Euler when } \bigl|\text{eig}\bigl((I - \Delta t A)^{-1}\bigr)\bigr| \le 1 . $$


Now we can diagnose Section 4.2.2 exactly. Recall the two eigenvalues of $A$, $\lambda \approx -1.97$ and $\lambda \approx -20.0$. The fast one demands $\Delta t \le 2/20.0 = 0.0999$ — and we used $\Delta t = 0.1$, a hair over the line.

In [ ]:
print('eigenvalues of A        ', np.linalg.eigvals(A))
print('forward Euler needs dt <= 2/|lambda|_max = %.5f\n' % (2/max(abs(np.linalg.eigvals(A)))))

print('   dt      max |eig(I + dt A)|    max |eig((I - dt A)^-1)|')
for dt in [0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.01]:
    gF = max(abs(np.linalg.eigvals(np.eye(2) + A*dt)))
    gB = max(abs(np.linalg.eigvals(np.linalg.inv(np.eye(2) - A*dt))))
    print('%6.2f        %8.4f  %s            %8.4f  %s'
          % (dt, gF, 'UNSTABLE' if gF > 1 else 'stable  ',
                 gB, 'UNSTABLE' if gB > 1 else 'stable'))

eigenvalues of A         [ -1.97203638 -20.01911219]
forward Euler needs dt <= 2/|lambda|_max = 0.09990

   dt      max |eig(I + dt A)|    max |eig((I - dt A)^-1)|
  0.20          3.0038  UNSTABLE              0.7172  stable
  0.10          1.0019  UNSTABLE              0.8353  stable
  0.05          0.9014  stable                0.9102  stable
  0.01          0.9803  stable                0.9807  stable

At $\Delta t = 0.1$ the forward-Euler amplification factor is $1.0019$ — barely above one, which is why the solution in Section 4.2.2 grew slowly rather than exploding. At $\Delta t = 0.2$ it is far above one. Backward Euler stays below one at every step size tested, as the stability region promised.


The same test can be run over a range of damping ratios, and it is worth reading the result carefully.

In [ ]:
print('   zeta     eig(A)                        max |eig(I + dt A)|  at dt = 0.1')
for dd in [0.25, 1.0, 1.75, 2.0, 20.0]:
    Ad = np.array([[0, 1], [-w**2, -2*dd*w]])
    ev = np.linalg.eigvals(Ad)
    gF = max(abs(np.linalg.eigvals(np.eye(2) + Ad*0.1)))
    print('%7.2f   %-28s  %10.4f   %s'
          % (dd, np.array2string(ev, precision = 2), gF, 'UNSTABLE' if gF > 1 else 'stable'))

   zeta     eig(A)                        max |eig(I + dt A)|  at dt = 0.1
   0.25   [-1.57+6.08j -1.57-6.08j]         1.0395   UNSTABLE
   1.00   [-6.28 -6.28]                     0.3717   stable
   1.75   [ -1.97 -20.02]                   1.0019   UNSTABLE
   2.00   [ -1.68 -23.45]                   1.3449   UNSTABLE
  20.00   [-1.57e-01 -2.51e+02]            24.1170   UNSTABLE

Only one row is stable, and it is not the one a physicist would guess. There are two distinct ways to fall outside the small disc. The lightly damped case $\zeta = 0.25$ has complex eigenvalues lying close to the imaginary axis — and the forward-Euler disc touches that axis only at the origin, so an oscillator with little damping is almost always outside it. At the other end, raising $\zeta$ above one makes the slow mode slower and the fast mode very much faster, until at $\zeta = 20$ the eigenvalues differ by a factor of sixteen hundred and the amplification factor is $24$.


A system whose eigenvalues differ by orders of magnitude like this is called stiff, and stiffness is the single most common reason for an explicit solver to crawl: the step size is dictated by the fastest mode even after that mode has decayed away and contributes nothing to the answer. A physically tamer system can therefore be numerically far harder. Implicit methods exist precisely for these problems, and general-purpose libraries offer both families — solve_ivp defaults to the explicit RK45, and switches to implicit methods such as Radau or BDF when asked.


4.5. A Nonlinear Example: the Pendulum¶

4.5.1. The Equation of Motion¶

Nothing so far required $f$ to be linear; the matrix form was a convenience. The pendulum shows the general case.


A point mass $m$ on a rigid massless rod of length $L$, with $\theta$ measured from the downward vertical, has kinetic and potential energy


$$ T = \tfrac12 m L^2 \dot\theta^2 , \qquad V = m g L\,(1 - \cos\theta) , $$


and the Euler-Lagrange equation applied to $\mathcal{L} = T - V$ gives


$$ \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot\theta} - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial\theta} = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \ddot\theta = \frac{g}{L}\sin\theta , $$


in which $g$ carries the sign of the gravitational acceleration along the coordinate direction — it is entered as a negative number, so that the equation reads $\ddot\theta = -|g|/L \cdot \sin\theta$ and the hanging position $\theta = 0$ is the stable one. Adding linear damping $-d\,\dot\theta$ and introducing $v = \dot\theta$ gives the first-order system


$$ \begin{aligned} \dot\theta &= v \\ \dot v &= \frac{g}{L}\sin\theta - d\,v \end{aligned} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\begin{bmatrix}\theta \\ v\end{bmatrix} = f\!\left(\begin{bmatrix}\theta \\ v\end{bmatrix}\right) . $$


The $\sin\theta$ makes this nonlinear, so there is no matrix $A$ and no closed-form solution. For small angles $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ and the equation reduces to the spring-mass-damper of Section 4.2 — which is exactly why that example is worth understanding first.


In code, $f$ becomes a function of $t$ and the state vector $y = [\theta, v]$, returning the list of derivatives. This is the interface every solver expects.

In [ ]:
def pendulum_ode(t, y, g, L, d):
    return [y[1],
            (g/L)*np.sin(y[0]) - d*y[1]]

4.5.2. Simulating It¶

With $g = -10$ and $L = 10$ the ratio $g/L = -1$, so the small-angle period is $2\pi\sqrt{L/|g|} = 2\pi$ seconds. The pendulum is released from $\theta = \pi/4$ at rest and followed for $50$ seconds, with light damping $d = 0.1$.

In [ ]:
# define physical constants
g = -10
L = 10
d = 0.1

# define time slices and initial condition
t = np.linspace(0, 50, 500)
y0 = [np.pi/4, 0]

pendulum_sol = solve_ivp(pendulum_ode, (0, 50), y0, t_eval = t, args = (g, L, d,))
y = pendulum_sol.y

print('theta(0)  = %7.4f' % y[0, 0])
print('theta(50) = %7.4f' % y[0, -1])
print('small-angle period  2*pi*sqrt(L/|g|) = %.4f s' % (2*np.pi*np.sqrt(L/abs(g))))

theta(50) =  0.0465

The left panel shows the familiar decaying oscillation. The right panel is the phase portrait, the trajectory drawn in the $(\theta, v)$ plane with time eliminated: it spirals inward to the origin, which is the hanging equilibrium. The three-dimensional plot shows how the two pictures are related — the phase portrait is the shadow of the trajectory looking down the time axis.

4.5.3. Forward Euler on a Nonlinear Problem¶

The Euler loop needs no modification for a nonlinear problem. There is no matrix to form, so $f$ is simply called at each step.

In [ ]:
dt = 0.1
n = int(50/dt)

yF = np.zeros((2, n + 1))
tF = np.arange(n + 1)*dt
yF[:, 0] = y0
for i in range(n):
    f = np.array(pendulum_ode(tF[i], yF[:, i], g, L, d))
    yF[:, i + 1] = yF[:, i] + dt*f

plt.plot(tF, yF[0, :], 'k', linewidth = 1.2)
plt.plot(t, y[0, :], 'r--', linewidth = 1.2)
plt.legend(['Forward Euler, $\\Delta t = 0.1$', 'solve_ivp'], fontsize = 11)
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('$t$', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('$\\theta$', fontsize = 12)
plt.show()

print('theta(50)   Forward Euler %8.4f     solve_ivp %8.4f\n' % (yF[0, -1], y[0, -1]))

# amplitude over the last ten seconds
print('amplitude for t in [40, 50]')
print('   Forward Euler  %.4f' % np.abs(yF[0, tF >= 40]).max())
print('   solve_ivp      %.4f' % np.abs(y[0, t >= 40]).max())

# linearize about theta = 0 and apply the eigenvalue test
Alin = np.array([[0, 1], [g/L, -d]])
print('\nlinearized eigenvalues   ', np.linalg.eigvals(Alin))
print('max |eig(I + dt Alin)|    %.10f' % max(abs(np.linalg.eigvals(np.eye(2) + Alin*dt))))

theta(50)   Forward Euler  -0.2332     solve_ivp   0.0465

amplitude for t in [40, 50]
   Forward Euler  0.6824
   solve_ivp      0.0976

linearized eigenvalues    [-0.05+0.99874922j -0.05-0.99874922j]
max |eig(I + dt Alin)|    1.0000000000

The two curves agree at first and then part company completely. Over the last ten seconds the reference solution has decayed to an amplitude of about $0.10$, while forward Euler is still swinging at $0.68$ — seven times too large. The method has not merely accumulated first-order error; it has lost the damping altogether.


The eigenvalue test says why. Linearizing about $\theta = 0$ gives $\lambda = -d/2 \pm i\sqrt{\omega_0^2 - d^2/4}$ with $\omega_0^2 = |g|/L$, and a line of algebra gives the forward-Euler amplification factor


$$ \bigl|1 + \lambda\Delta t\bigr|^2 = 1 - d\,\Delta t + \omega_0^2\,\Delta t^2 . $$


The middle term is the physical damping, the last term is the energy the method injects, and with $d = 0.1$, $\Delta t = 0.1$ and $\omega_0 = 1$ they cancel exactly — the printed factor is $1$ to machine precision. Forward Euler is reporting a pendulum that never stops swinging, because its own numerical energy production happens to match the damper.


Remove the damping and only the injection is left. An undamped pendulum conserves energy and its linearized eigenvalues are purely imaginary, $\lambda = \pm i\omega_0$; the formula above becomes $|1 + \lambda\Delta t|^2 = 1 + \omega_0^2\Delta t^2 > 1$ for every step size. Forward Euler cannot help adding energy to an oscillator.

In [ ]:
dt = 0.05
n = int(50/dt)

yE = np.zeros((2, n + 1))
tE = np.arange(n + 1)*dt
yE[:, 0] = y0
for i in range(n):
    f = np.array(pendulum_ode(tE[i], yE[:, i], g, L, 0))     # d = 0, no damping
    yE[:, i + 1] = yE[:, i] + dt*f

energy = 0.5*yE[1, :]**2 + (abs(g)/L)*(1 - np.cos(yE[0, :]))

plt.figure(figsize = (12, 4))
plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.plot(tE, yE[0, :], 'k', linewidth = 1.0)
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('$t$', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('$\\theta$', fontsize = 12)
plt.title('undamped pendulum, Forward Euler', fontsize = 11)

plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.plot(tE, energy, 'k', linewidth = 1.2)
plt.grid(True)
plt.xlabel('$t$', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('energy per unit mass', fontsize = 12)
plt.title('energy should be constant', fontsize = 11)
plt.show()

print('energy at t = 0    %.5f' % energy[0])
print('energy at t = 50   %.5f   (a factor of %.1f)' % (energy[-1], energy[-1]/energy[0]))

energy at t = 0    0.29289
energy at t = 50   1.70868   (a factor of 5.8)

The amplitude grows steadily and the energy — which the physics requires to be constant — rises by a factor of nearly six over fifty seconds. No step size removes this; it only slows it down. A problem with this structure calls for a method whose stability region contains part of the imaginary axis, such as a Runge-Kutta method, or a symplectic integrator designed to conserve energy exactly.




5. Boundary Value Problems¶

5.1. Two-Point Boundary Value Problems¶

5.1.1. Initial Value or Boundary Value¶

Chapter 4 solved the initial value problem: the entire state is known at $t = 0$, and the differential equation says how to march forward. Every method there was a rule for getting from $x_k$ to $x_{k+1}$, and the solution was built one step at a time.


Many problems in engineering are not posed that way. Consider the steady temperature in a rod whose two ends are held at fixed temperatures, or the deflection of a beam that is pinned at both ends. The governing equation is still a second-order differential equation, but the two conditions needed to pin down its solution are given at opposite ends of the interval:


$$ u''(x) = f(x), \qquad a < x < b, \qquad u(a) = \alpha, \quad u(b) = \beta . $$


This is a two-point boundary value problem. Nothing can be marched: at $x = a$ we know $u$ but not $u'$, so there is no complete state to step forward from. The value of the solution in the middle of the interval depends on both ends at once.


That single difference changes the numerical strategy completely.

  • In an initial value problem the unknowns are computed one after another, each from the ones before it.
  • In a boundary value problem the unknowns are all coupled, and must be computed simultaneously.

A boundary value problem therefore does not turn into a loop; it turns into a system of algebraic equations. And the way to turn a differential equation into algebraic equations is already in hand: replace the derivatives by the finite differences of Chapter 2.

5.1.2. The Model Problem¶

We take the simplest representative problem,


$$ u''(x) = f(x), \qquad 0 < x < 1, \qquad u(0) = \alpha, \quad u(1) = \beta , $$


which describes the steady-state temperature $u$ along a rod of unit length and unit conductivity, heated internally at the rate $-f(x)$, with the two ends held at the prescribed temperatures $\alpha$ and $\beta$. The same equation describes the small deflection of a loaded string and the electrostatic potential of a given charge distribution, and the numerical treatment is identical in all three cases.


For a test we choose a problem whose answer is known,


$$ f(x) = -\pi^2 \sin(\pi x), \qquad \alpha = 0, \quad \beta = 1 , \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad u(x) = \sin(\pi x) + x , $$


as is verified by differentiating twice and checking the two end values. Everything below is written for a general $f$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$; the exact solution is used only to measure the error.

In [ ]:
# the rod:  u'' = f(x),  u(0) = alpha,  u(1) = beta
def f(x):
    return -np.pi**2*np.sin(np.pi*x)

def uexact(x):                 # the exact solution, used only to check the error
    return np.sin(np.pi*x) + x

alpha = 0
beta = 1

5.2. The Finite Difference Method¶

5.2.1. From Derivatives to a Matrix¶

Lay down the same uniform grid as in Section 2.5,


$$ x_k = k\,\Delta x, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, n , \qquad \Delta x = \frac{1}{n} , $$


and write $u_k$ for the approximation to $u(x_k)$. The two end values are not unknown at all: the boundary conditions give $u_0 = \alpha$ and $u_n = \beta$ directly.


$$ \begin{aligned} k = 0: \quad & u_0 = \alpha \\ k = n: \quad & u_{n} = \beta \end{aligned} $$


The unknowns are the $n - 1$ interior values $u_1, \dots, u_{n-1}$. At each interior point, replace $u''$ by the three-point central formula of Section 2.4.1:


$$ \frac{u_{k-1} - 2u_k + u_{k+1}}{\Delta x^2} = f(x_k), \qquad k = 1, 2, \dots, n-1 . $$


That is one equation per interior point, and there are exactly as many equations as unknowns. The differential equation has become a linear system. To see its structure, write the equations out one by one, multiplied through by $\Delta x^2$ for the moment so that the pattern is easy to read:


$$ \begin{aligned} k = 1: \quad & u_0 - 2u_1 + u_2 = \Delta x^2 f(x_1), \\ k = 2: \quad & u_1 - 2u_2 + u_3 = \Delta x^2 f(x_2), \\ & \;\;\vdots \\ k = n-2: \quad & u_{n-3} - 2u_{n-2} + u_{n-1} = \Delta x^2 f(x_{n-2}), \\ k = n-1: \quad & u_{n-2} - 2u_{n-1} + u_n = \Delta x^2 f(x_{n-1}). \end{aligned} $$


Each equation involves exactly three consecutive grid values, the point itself and its two neighbours, with the coefficients $1, -2, 1$.


Two of these equations are special. The one at $k = 1$ contains $u_0$, and the one at $k = n-1$ contains $u_n$; both of those are known numbers, $\alpha$ and $\beta$. A known quantity does not belong on the side of the unknowns, so it is subtracted from both sides, and the first and last equations become


$$ \begin{aligned} k = 1: \quad & -2u_1 + u_2 = \Delta x^2 f(x_1) - \alpha, \\ k = n-1: \quad & u_{n-2} - 2u_{n-1} = \Delta x^2 f(x_{n-1}) - \beta . \end{aligned} $$


The interior equations, $k = 2, \dots, n-2$, are unchanged. Now every equation contains only the unknowns $u_1, \dots, u_{n-1}$ on the left, and only known quantities on the right.


The system is assembled into a matrix in the usual way: the $k$-th equation becomes the $k$-th row, and the coefficient of $u_j$ in that equation goes into column $j$. From the list above, row $k$ therefore has the entry $1$ in column $k-1$, the entry $-2$ in column $k$, and the entry $1$ in column $k+1$, and all other entries are zero. In the first row the entry in column $0$ is missing, and in the last row the entry in column $n$ is missing, because the values they would multiply, $u_0$ and $u_n$, have been moved to the right-hand side. Dividing by $\Delta x^2$ again and writing the system as $Au = b$ with $u = (u_1, \dots, u_{n-1})^T$,


$$ \underbrace{ \frac{1}{\Delta x^2} \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 & & & \\ 1 & -2 & 1 & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ & & & 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} }_{A} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \\ \vdots \\ u_{n-2} \\ u_{n-1} \end{bmatrix} }_{u} = \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} f(x_1) - \alpha/\Delta x^2 \\ f(x_2) \\ \vdots \\ f(x_{n-2}) \\ f(x_{n-1}) - \beta/\Delta x^2 \end{bmatrix} }_{b} . $$


Reading the matrix row by row against the equations above shows where every entry comes from: the diagonal $-2$ is the coefficient of $u_k$ in the $k$-th equation, the two $1$'s beside it are the coefficients of $u_{k-1}$ and $u_{k+1}$, and the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in the right-hand side are the boundary values that left the first and last equations.


The matrix is the discrete Laplacian $(1, -2, 1)/\Delta x^2$ met in Section 2.4.1, now written out for a whole grid. It is tridiagonal: every row contains at most three nonzero entries, because the stencil couples each point only to its two immediate neighbours. The boundary values appear nowhere in the matrix and only in the first and last entries of the right-hand side: changing $\alpha$ or $\beta$ changes $b$, not $A$.


This is the difference from Chapter 4 in one sentence: a time-stepping method applies the stencil sequentially, computing each new value from values already known, whereas a boundary value method assembles it into a matrix and solves once, because no interior value can be computed before the others.

In [ ]:
n = 20                                      # number of subintervals
x = np.linspace(0, 1, n + 1)
dx = x[1] - x[0]

print('grid spacing   dx = %.4f' % dx)
print('unknowns       n - 1 = %d' % (n - 1))

grid spacing   dx = 0.0500
unknowns       n - 1 = 19

5.2.2. Building and Solving the System¶

The matrix is built one row at a time, which is the literal transcription of "one finite difference equation per interior point". The two if statements are there only because the first and last rows have no left or no right neighbour.

In [ ]:
A = np.zeros((n - 1, n - 1))

# one row of A is one finite difference equation
for i in range(n - 1):
    A[i, i] = -2
    if i > 0:
        A[i, i - 1] = 1
    if i < n - 2:
        A[i, i + 1] = 1

A = A/dx**2

print('top left corner of A, in units of 1/dx^2')
print(A[0:4, 0:4]*dx**2)

top left corner of A, in units of 1/dx^2
[[-2.  1.  0.  0.]
 [ 1. -2.  1.  0.]
 [ 0.  1. -2.  1.]
 [ 0.  0.  1. -2.]]

The right-hand side is the source term sampled at the interior points, with the two boundary values subtracted at the two ends. One call to a linear solver then produces all $n - 1$ interior values at once, and the two known end values are put back in place.

In [ ]:
b = np.zeros(n - 1)

for i in range(n - 1):
    b[i] = f(x[i + 1])

# the two known boundary values move to the right-hand side
b[0] = b[0] - alpha/dx**2
b[-1] = b[-1] - beta/dx**2

u = np.zeros(n + 1)
u[0] = alpha
u[-1] = beta
u[1:-1] = np.linalg.solve(A, b)

print('max error  %9.2e' % np.max(np.abs(u - uexact(x))))

max error   2.06e-03
In [ ]:
# Plot
xf = np.linspace(0, 1, 400)

plt.plot(xf, uexact(xf), 'k--')
plt.plot(x, u, 'ro', markersize = 5)
plt.xlim(0, 1)
plt.ylim(0, 2)
plt.xlabel('x', fontsize = 12)
plt.ylabel('u(x)', fontsize = 12)
plt.legend(['exact solution', 'finite difference'], fontsize = 12)
plt.show()

Twenty subintervals already reproduce the solution to about two parts in a thousand, and the computed points are indistinguishable from the exact curve by eye. Note what was not needed: no initial slope, no time stepping, no stability restriction on the step size. The boundary value problem is not integrated, it is solved.


This chapter closes the circle opened in Chapter 2. A derivative was replaced by a difference of neighbouring values; that difference, applied at every point of a grid and collected into a matrix, converts a differential equation into a linear system. The finite difference method for partial differential equations is this same construction carried out in more than one variable.




6. Partial Differential Equations¶

6.1. Introduction to Partial Differential Equations¶

6.1.1. Two Independent Variables¶

Every problem so far has had one independent variable: time in Chapter 4, position in Chapter 5. A partial differential equation involves a function of several variables, here $u(x, t)$ of space and time, and its partial derivatives. The three classical examples are


$$ \begin{align*} u_t &= \alpha\,u_{xx} \quad \text{(heat equation, diffusion)}, \\\\ u_{tt} &= c^2\,u_{xx} \quad \text{(wave equation)}, \\\\ u_{xx} + u_{yy} &= 0 \quad \text{(Laplace equation, equilibrium)} \end{align*} $$


Chapter 5 was already the last kind in one dimension: with no time in the problem, $u'' = f$ described equilibrium. This chapter takes the heat equation and puts the time back in.


Remark. We discretize with finite differences, replacing each derivative by a difference quotient, as in Chapters 2 and 5. The finite element and finite volume methods, standard in structural mechanics and fluid dynamics, reach a similar system of algebraic equations by a different route.

6.1.2. The One-Dimensional Heat Equation¶

The model problem is the transient temperature of a thin rod of length $L$,


$$ \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \alpha\,\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} , \qquad 0 < x < L , \qquad t > 0 , $$


where $\alpha > 0$ is the thermal diffusivity. The equation says that a point heats up in proportion to how much colder it is than the average of its two neighbours — which is exactly what the second difference of Section 2.4.1 measures.


Because both a time derivative and a space derivative appear, the problem needs both kinds of data met so far: an initial condition $u(x, 0) = u_0(x)$ as in Chapter 4, and boundary conditions at the two ends for all $t$ as in Chapter 5. Here both ends are held at zero, $u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0$ — an ice bath at each end.


Discretize both variables,


$$ x_i = i\,\Delta x \quad (i = 0, \dots, N_x) , \qquad t_n = n\,\Delta t \quad (n = 0, 1, 2, \dots) , \qquad u_i^n \approx u(x_i, t_n) , $$


the subscript for space and the superscript for time. The computed solution is no longer a curve but a table: one row per time level, each row a snapshot of the whole rod.


For a test we take the initial temperature $u_0(x) = \sin(\pi x / L)$, which is an eigenfunction of $\partial^2/\partial x^2$ and therefore decays in place without changing shape:


$$ u(x, t) = e^{-\alpha \pi^2 t / L^2}\,\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right) . $$


Every approximation below can be compared against this.

In [ ]:
# the rod:  u_t = alpha u_xx,  u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0
L = 1.0                                 # length of the rod
alpha = 1.0                             # thermal diffusivity
T = 0.1                                 # total simulation time

def uexact(x, t):                       # used only to check the error
    return np.exp(-alpha*np.pi**2*t/L**2)*np.sin(np.pi*x/L)

Nx = 50                                 # number of spatial segments
dx = L/Nx
x = np.linspace(0, L, Nx + 1)

6.2. The Explicit Method¶

6.2.1. Forward in Time, Central in Space¶

Replace each derivative by the formula already derived for it. For the time derivative use the forward difference of Section 2.2, which is the forward Euler method of Chapter 4; for the space derivative use the three-point central stencil of Section 2.4.1, the same one that built the matrix in Chapter 5:


$$ \frac{u_i^{n+1} - u_i^n}{\Delta t} = \alpha\left(\frac{u_{i+1}^n - 2u_i^n + u_{i-1}^n}{\Delta x^2}\right) . $$


Only one quantity refers to the new time level, so it can be solved for directly:


$$ u_i^{n+1} = u_i^n + r\left(u_{i+1}^n - 2u_i^n + u_{i-1}^n\right) , \qquad r = \frac{\alpha\,\Delta t}{\Delta x^2} . $$


This is the explicit method, or FTCS (forward time, central space). Each new value is a weighted average of three old ones, no system has to be solved, and the whole method is one line inside a loop. The single dimensionless mesh ratio $r$ contains everything about the discretization, and the entire behaviour of the scheme turns out to depend on it alone.


The update formula is one line, but it is applied once for every interior point. Writing it out for $i = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ at a fixed time level $n$ shows what a single sweep of the loop does:


$$ \begin{aligned} i = 1: \quad u_1^{n+1} &= u_1^n + r\left(u_2^n - 2u_1^n + u_0^n\right), \\ i = 2: \quad u_2^{n+1} &= u_2^n + r\left(u_3^n - 2u_2^n + u_1^n\right), \\ i = 3: \quad u_3^{n+1} &= u_3^n + r\left(u_4^n - 2u_3^n + u_2^n\right), \\ &\;\;\vdots \\ i = N_x - 1: \quad u_{N_x-1}^{n+1} &= u_{N_x-1}^n + r\left(u_{N_x}^n - 2u_{N_x-1}^n + u_{N_x-2}^n\right). \end{aligned} $$


Three things are visible in this list that the compact formula hides.


Every line has the same shape, and only the subscript moves by one from line to line. That is the inner loop, for i in range(1, N_x), with the subscript as the array index.


Every quantity on the right-hand side carries the superscript $n$, and only the quantity on the left carries $n+1$. The whole right-hand side is therefore known before the sweep begins, and the lines can be evaluated in any order; none of them needs a result from another line. This is why the method is called explicit, and why the code must read from the old array and write into a new one rather than overwrite in place.


The first line uses $u_0^n$ and the last uses $u_{N_x}^n$. These are the boundary values, which are never computed by the formula but supplied by the boundary conditions; the loop runs over $i = 1, \dots, N_x - 1$ and leaves the two ends alone.


Once the sweep is complete, the new level replaces the old one, $n \leftarrow n + 1$, and the same list of lines is evaluated again. That is the outer loop.

In [ ]:
r = 0.45                                # mesh ratio
dt = r*dx**2/alpha
Nt = int(round(T/dt))

print('dx = %.4f    dt = %.2e' % (dx, dt))
print('r  = %.2f    number of time steps = %d' % (r, Nt))

dx = 0.0200    dt = 1.80e-04
r  = 0.45    number of time steps = 556
In [ ]:
